subtopic: BRUSSELS-REPORTED CRITICISM OF CANADIAN PAVILION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BRUSSELS-REPORTED CRITICISM OF CANADIAN PAVILION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have an editorial from the issue of that great family journal and independent political newspaper known as the Toronto Telegram of Saturday, May 17. The editorial is entitled, "Show Window in Brussels." I should like to ask the minister if he has read the editorial. Second, does the minister intend to take the advice given him and catch a plane to Brussels to straighten out matters over there?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: BRUSSELS-REPORTED CRITICISM OF CANADIAN PAVILION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. I have read the editorial. I would have no objection to going to Brussels immediately, but at the moment I do not see that any good purpose would be served by my doing so. The Canadian pavilion at the world fair at Brussels was designed and planned about two years ago. When we assumed office last summer the plans had been completed in final form. I was in Brussels last September. I saw the pavilion in the course of construction, and was given some indication of its general lay-out and the grounds surrounding it.

Subsequently, since the exhibition has been opened, statements have appeared in the press and some letters have been sent to me objecting to certain things over there. Objection has been taken to the meals served in the restaurant; there has been a query as to whether the ramp which leads to the second floor is a suitable method of gaining access to the second floor; some objection has been taken to the size of the building, and to the nature of the exhibits shown therein. It is extremely difficult, when you are dealing with a thing like this, to be sure what should be done. There is a difference of opinion amongst people with regard to art and architecture; not all people can be completely satisfied with regard to a pavilion such as this. I am no expert on art. I do not understand surrealism or modern painting. I did appreciate, however, a cartoon which appeared during the election campaign giving a surrealistic vision of Canada.
In so far as this particular pavilion is concerned, I have had a first-hand account from a competent observer who has just returned from Brussels and who spent five days there looking at the various pavilions, the Canadian pavilion in particular. If I have your permission, sir, I should like to report that Mrs. Michener told me yesterday that she made an extensive tour of all the pavilions at the world fair, and that the Canadian pavilion is a credit to Canada. She said that in her opinion the entire Canadian exhibit had been imaginatively planned and that it gives an adequate picture of the country as a whole. This, she said, is not true of the pavilions of other smaller countries. The exhibit of Canadian industries and arts is a better representation than that of the United States. She particularly mentioned the excellence of the fisheries exhibit. The automatic fish are so lifelike that a visitor attempted to feed them bread crumbs before she discovered her error. The gardens surrounding the building have been well laid out.

subtopic: BRUSSELS-REPORTED CRITICISM OF CANADIAN PAVILION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; surely this is not proper procedure by the ministry in answering a question. The minister has transgressed the rules by not being concise and relevant, and has transgressed on some other grounds which you, Mr. Speaker, could not fail to observe. He has transgressed the bounds of good taste as well.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BRUSSELS-REPORTED CRITICISM OF CANADIAN PAVILION
speechtext:
The minister has proceeded on his own responsibility. I feel this is not a matter that can be dealt with satisfactorily in the question period, and there will be an
Inquiries of the Ministry opportunity to discuss the pros and cons of the Canadian exhibit in the debate that is now taking place.

Mr. Speaker, even though I have only one minute left to me, I will try to make use of it.
Yesterday, during the debate, I spoke of this extraordinary business slowdown which displays at the same time inflationary tendencies. I stated my belief that taxes could be cut down, but I had not quite had my say. The objection will possibly be raised that new tax cuts would increase the danger of inflation. My suggestion is this. Extraordinary times call for extraordinary measures, and the government could take them just as it did during the war. At that time, because of the difficulties of the period, the government fixed prices. To my mind, the source of all this difficulty is instalment buying of luxury goods. I am of the opinion that the government could declare a state of emergency and order that no credit is to be allowed purchasers unless they can pay 25 per cent down.
Price control could also be established on food, because if we allow the prices of food to go up, workers will apply for raises in salary, followed by further price increases; thereby creating a vicious circle from which there will be no escape.

I take this occasion on behalf of those of us who have been veterans of this house since June 10 to welcome those members who are newly elected since March 31. If they derive as much enjoyment and pleasure out of service in this place as we have who were elected on June 10 they are about to enjoy an enriching and rewarding experience. They will find also that their participation in the proceedings of this house will not only be welcomed but will be encouraged.
I should like to comment upon the great contributions that have been made to parliamentary debate in the last few days by those of the newly-elected members who have already spoken on the address. I want to compliment, too, the 50 representatives from ancient French Canada. Their arrival in this house when it opened last week entitles me I think, to call myself a prophet. I refer to what I said on the occasion of my maiden speech in this house on October 21, 1957. In Hansard of that date, at page 202, I am recorded as having said:
At this moment on this side of the house there are not as many representatives of my French Canadian friends as I should like to see, but in the expectation that when the first opportunity presents itself this situation will be corrected we are holding in reserve as many as 50 places to accommodate the newcomers.
At that time I think there were approximately nine members from the province of Quebec on this side of the house.
I continued:
In the meantime, it will be the proud privilege of all of us on this side of the house to see to it that the ancient rights and privileges of French Canada are jealously maintained and safeguarded.
The Address-Mr. Maloney (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to quote an excerpt from the first speech I made in this house, on October 21, 1957:
At the moment, on this side of the house there are not as many representatives of my French Canadian friends as I should like to see but, in the expectation that when the first opportunity presents itself this situation will be corrected, we are holding in reserve as many as fifty places to accommodate the newcomers.
This proves that I am almost a prophet. (Text):
The success of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec was nothing more than confirmation of what we had always contended, namely that we were the party of all of the people of this country, the party of the Anglo-Saxon, the party of the French and the party of all the other ethnic groups in the country's population.
I would like at this stage to extend my warmest congratulations to the newly appointed Secretary of State (Mr. Courte-manche), and the newly apopinted Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley). Their past service in this house fully warrants our confident prediction that their service in these new and important posts will be of a very high calibre indeed. I should also like to express my congratulations to the newly named Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough).
Those of us who are on the Conservative side of the house are here today in such large numbers for a variety of reasons, and I do not for a moment intend to attempt to exhaust all those reasons. We are here today in the first place because we served our country in the fold of the Conservative party under the leadership of an inspired and dedicated Canadian, under the leadership of a Prime Minister whose whole background in his profession and as a parliamentarian, has been dedicated to the rights, under the law, of the average, ordinary, humble people of this country.
We are here today because of a record of accomplishment and of promises fulfilled that has not been equalled in so short a time in the history of this country, and we can boast of that record since June 10 last. We are here also because of the prominent and the influential role of youth in the councils of our party. In the twenty-third parliament of this country 35 of our members were under 40 years of age; and while I am not sure as to the accuracy of these statistics, I am under the impression that we have on our side of the house today almost 100 members under the age of 40, which gives to our

The Address-Mr. Maloney party an air of permanence and to the people of Canada a confidence in the country's future under our leadership.
I think we are also here today because of the aggressive steps the government has taken to solve the unemployment problem of this country. I should like to say a word about the matter of unemployment, because some of those from the opposition parties who have spoken in this debate before me have seen fit to speak about the question. There has been much discussion of it both inside and outside the house since early last fall. To hear some hon. members, and others who do not have the privilege of being members of this house, you would think we were in the middle of a depression. To hear others you would almost think they were disappointed with the idea that the government might succeed in getting us out of the situation.
I do not think any hon. member, regardless of his political party, can fairly deny that this government has done everything that any government could possibly have done. There has been a reallocation of public works funds in order to apply directly and as quickly as possible the full force of an extra $200 million, in addition to the last calendar year's expenditures, to our economy. No one can deny that the effect of this wise and forceful measure has been most positive and beneficial. In housing alone the result has been to more than double the number of starts in the first quarter of the year, 17,360 units this year compared with 8,410 last year. This stimulus has spread through many other facets of the economy, particularly those closely related to housing. As I say, the results are already evident and will begin to show even more powerfully over the next month or so.
I am one of those who believe that the policy-and in some places it has been erected into a policy-of viewing with constant alarm does only disservice to the country. It must be apparent to the members of the house, that the employment situation in Canada now is certainly much more buoyant than the prophets of doom had led us to expect last winter. At that time, when the Minister of Labour assured the house that he was confident that the natural buoyancy of our economy would reassert itself, he was shouted down by those who wanted to cry havoc! Today there is every indication that his confidence has been borne out and that their pessimism besides being destructive has neither been a fair nor accurate analysis of the situation.
The most recent dominion bureau of statistics figure was 590,000. This is a high figure for unemployment, about 10 per cent of the labour force. But people who say this is a depression figure should keep in mind

that a conservative estimate of unemployment during the depression period was from 20 per cent to 25 per cent. I do not know what a liberal estimate might be; perhaps considerably higher.

And he got all the A's. A further dominion bureau of statistics report will be made available within a day or so, and then it will be made evident whether this figure of 590,000 was in truth the peak of the unemployment, as we on this side predicted it was during the recent election.
According to registration figures of the national employment service, there has been a decrease in registration since March 13 of more than 171,729, which surely is not suggestive of a depression. National registration figures are being held up at the moment because of the extension of seasonal benefits for a further six weeks. At the end of that time the current rate of decline of approximately 40,000 a week should be even sharper. Thus, while there are still problems facing the economy, the picture is not nearly so dark as some of our friends would have had the people of this country believe in the weeks that preceded the election when, in the press and on television, they made the air ring with their sad lamentations.
At this point I should like to offer my own personal tribute to the Minister of Labour for his staunch and steadfast demeanour in the face of adverse, uninformed and unfair criticism. I know that various measures of the government have been criticized on the ground that they would not individually solve unemployment. This point is true and well taken but only as far as it goes. These measures must be taken collectively and adjudged in their cumulative effect. I have in mind such measures as bringing forward immense public works expenditures, extending seasonal benefits, stimulating housing and construction and embarking upon large development programs in the north. Surely had these not been undertaken our economy would certainly not now be showing the buoyancy which is once again becoming evident. And it is certainly true to say that had the application of a tight money policy and high immigration, sponsored by the former administration, been left in effect, combined with the do-nothing attitude shown by that administration under similar circumstances

in 1955 then, Mr. Speaker, the general condition of the economy at this moment might well have borne out the most dire predictions of the prophets of doom.
Another reason to account for the large numbers who sit in support of the government in this house is the doctrine of national unity that was preached and practised by the Conservative party. Our philosophy as propounded and developed for the benefit of the people of Canada in the weeks that preceded the election of March 31 was the same for every part of the country. All of us who spoke in support of the party prior to the election had no qualms, no apprehensions about saying out west what we said in the maritimes, about saying in Ontario what we said in Quebec. That was good Conservative philosophy, and in following this course we were only adhering to the oldest traditions of our party.
I think too we must not ignore the representative character of our party. We were prior to the election and are today able to make boasts such as these, boasts of which we are very proud. Ours is the only party that can boast of having the first Chinese member in the person of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung), the first Italian member in the person of the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Martini), the first Danish member; of having appointed the first Icelander and the first native Indian to the Senate; the first cabinet minister who is a woman; the first cabinet minister of Ukrainian racial origin. Indeed, we can boast of six hon. members in the house of Ukrainian origin, and all sitting on the right side of the house, too.
These were boasts of which we were proud. These were boasts which the Conservative party was able to voice from coast to coast. In other words, the governing party in this country today is a party of diversity. It is a party whose inner councils are enriched by the contributions made to them by people of all walks of life, of all races, of all classes and of all creeds. It is only right that the governing party of our country should be a party of diversity because the nation itself is a nation of diversity, and it is never tedious to advert to that diversity and to comment upon it.
About two hundred years ago there were by today's standards and in contrast a handful of French Canadians numbering only 65,000 or 70,000. The pride of that small group of people in their race, their language, their culture, their religion and their customs was so strong that even though they were cut off from all contact and all national ties with the country of their origin they have
The Address-Mr. Maloney over a span of two centuries developed such a firm and lasting national spirit that it has not only permeated the province of Quebec but has gone with French Canadians who have migrated to other parts of Canada and to the United States of America as well, and their number in Canada today has grown to at least five million.
On the other hand, the political framework by which the French Canadian was to see the fulfilment of his ambition to retain his own national identity was not his own invention or handiwork at all. Long before the close of the American revolution people of British stock residing in what is now the United States of America, and to whom we refer historically as united empire loyalists, preferred to give up their established homes and to move north so as to be accorded the privilege of continuing to live under the British crown. They were not in this country very long before they voiced their demands for British institutions, an elective assembly, habeas corpus, Magna Carta, trial by jury and all the other adornments and safeguards of the criminal law to which we are so long accustomed.
At that stage in our country's history these two great races were living side by side. It suited the French Canadian because he had the assurance of his right to retain what he was so fiercely anxious to retain, his religion, his language, the traditions of his race. In the case of the English they in most cases had given up established homes and businesses to come to a country that at that time had by today's standards nothing to offer except the security of the British crown and British traditions. Over long years of trial and error the two races continued the process of living side by side; and as this process of living together continued there was, all the time, developing in this country a nationality that was distinctively Canadian, a nationality that was making us different from any other country and any other people in the world.
But that was not to be the end of the story of this country. More was to come; more was to be added to it. Attracted by this complete lack of uniformity, attracted by this diversity which was our national characteristic were thousands upon thousands of people whose racial origins were to be found in the countries of central and eastern Europe and the Baltic states. They brought with them to this country their ancient cultures, their ancient traditions and customs. Each of them in its turn was to enrich our life, to add to it and to make the Canadian nationality something greater, something that it had not been before.

The Address-Mr. Maloney
When I think of some of these people who have come to this country from central and eastern Europe and the Baltic states; when I stop to think of some of the contributions they have made to the development of Canada and the richness they have brought to it, such thoughts as these go through my mind. I think of the people from the Baltic states, and I call to mind their terrible persecution as recently as June, 1940, and the frightful mass deportation of the Baltic peoples. They were taken out of their homes and the security of their countries and deported to the slave labour camps of Siberia. Husbands were separated from wives, families were broken up, brothers and sisters were separated, children were taken from their parents, and all were cruelly transported to slavery in Siberia where they now languish, some living only in the hope that their death will come all too soon.
When I think along these lines I think too of the Polish people, of the land of St. Casimir, their patron saint. I think of him as not only the patron saint of that country but one who might well be the patron saint of all who aspire to serve in public life, a saint who was the son of a powerful and noble king, a brother of not one but of two kings. On earth he was a young man who occupied a position of power, authority and influence. It is interesting as one reads his life to note that he used his position of power, authority and influence to help the downtrodden, the disconsolate and the poor. St. Casimir of Poland could well be an example to all of us in the parliament of Canada today who attempt to serve the people of our country, particularly the humblest, most ordinary people of the country.
I think too of the contributions that have been made to this country by people from Ukraine, bleeding and oppressed Ukraine, persecuted for centuries, never to lose its ethnic identity. I think of the great mass emigration of Ukrainians to this country in the late nineteenth century, their contribution to the growth of the west, to the construction of the railroads. I think of them coming here to escape economic oppression and settling in the west. I think of their piety so great that before they built their homes they built their churches; and they built their churches even before having ministers and priests to minister to their needs. I think of the great Ukrainians who today All such important roles in our country; the lawyers, doctors, parliamentarians on every level, and I think how greatly our life here has been enriched by them.

I think of the Hungarians and the frightful revolution of 1956 when, after ten years of communist indoctrination, even the youth stood up to fight and die as martyrs against the oppression of the Bolshevik tyrants. I think of people like Cardinal Mindzenty, a living martyr in the cause of freedom.
These then are some of the people who have come to our country in recent times and have served to enrich our life and culture. I think too of the Czechs, the Slovaks, the Croatians, the Serbs and the Byelorussians and all those people who now live under the heel of communist domination. These people were all given a message of hope when our Prime Minister, last December in Winnipeg, speaking to an audience of Ukrainians said this:
I am thinking, too, tonight of Canadians whose origins lie in countries which are likewise unfree to pursue their own aspirations-the Baltic states, eastern European countries such as Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia, which live in the shadow of tyranny. Never will we abandon the hope that justice will be done, that the irrepressible forces of human freedom will triumph.
He went on to say:	,
As a guarantee of good faith if the U.S.S.R. would show the sincerity of its protestations for peace, if it would grant free elections in those countries under its captive control and would free the untold numbers who are in slave camps, then the free world could move forward to early discussions designed to ameliorate the causes of discord and suspicion.
These people are teaching us a lesson. They are reminding us of the potential dangers that lie ahead. I can do no better in describing what I now mean than to use the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he spoke a few months ago in Toronto to an audience of Lithuanians. He said this:
From the sorrow of those whose freedom has been submerged, from the tragedy of those who are forced to live under serfdom by a government not of their own choice, we have derived a new determination, a sadder but wiser sense of direction in our own lives. Ever mindful of the fate of subjugated peoples, we know that in the enjoyment of our liberties, we must never become complacent, self-satisfied or apathetic. Our democracy is a virile and creative system, and its spirit is nowhere more alive than in the hearts of those who know only too well the cruel realities of oppression.
The election campaign which ended on March 31 was a great adventure in democracy in which all of us here present had the privilege of participating. I can recall numerous occasions when representatives of opposing political parties were invited to mingle with these people in their halls on their national days or to commemorate with them some great event in their history. I can recall how Liberals, Conservatives, and C.C.F.

used to foregather there under circumstances that were completely nonpolitical. When we spoke to such audiences they were witnessing something that was unknown in their homeland, the representatives of opposing political parties standing side by side. We, in our turn, we who aspired to public life, by being present with them, were reminded of the need to recall the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, never to become indifferent or apathetic.
When we came to their meetings and joined with them in their national celebrations we were reminded of the real purpose of our democracy and of the great election campaign in which we were engaged. We were reminded of the greatness of our democratic system, with its two mighty arms, the one to govern and the other to oppose; one charged with the responsibility of administering the affairs of the country, the other charged with the responsibility of holding that administration up to the bright glare of criticism, examination and scrutiny,-both arms equally important, equally indispensable. It gave to all of us now on the Conservative side of the house who had the privilege of seeing such things a great respect and a great admiration for those who fulfil the important role of opposition. It recalled to our minds words this house has already heard from the Prime Minister, spoken first in days when he was in the opposition and which he reiterated as Prime Minister of the country. When speaking to the Empire club in Toronto in 1949 he said:
"Parliament will only remain the guardian of free institutions as long as His Majesty's loyal opposition is fully responsible and effective in the discharge of its functions."
Those were words of inspiration to us all. We on this side of the house, numerically more powerful I suppose than any government in the history of the country, are very sensitive to the importance of the role of the left arm of democracy in this place. It is not judged by its quantity. It is not judged numerically. It is judged by the quality of the contribution it makes in fulfilling the role of opposition. We have attempted so far to demonstrate our respect for the opposition. We have announced that it is our intention to appoint an opposition member to chair the important committee on public accounts. We made no effort whatever to prevent recognition, as a separate group in this house, of the handful of members of the C.C.F. These are some indications of the respect and admiration we have for an opposition that fulfils its proper role.
In conclusion, may I say that we on all sides of this house can face the future with the mandate of the people fresh in our minds,
The Address-Mr. Houck in the confident hope that working together and each fulfilling our respective functions we will assist in solving the problems that now face the country and look to the future which we all know to be vast and limitless.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honoured custom not only in this house but in all legislatures to congratulate the Speaker. I think it is a good custom. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and I am not boasting, that I have had a lot of experience under various speakers. I have the utmost respect for you because of your experience. I have always appreciated your friendship and your leadership, especially in the last parliament when at times difficult circumstances arose and you ruled in a very fine way. I want to say as well, Mr. Speaker, that I think you have the qualities that make for a good speaker. You certainly have the ability. You have integrity, and you have leadership ability. You have another quality that I think should be present in every speaker, and that is not only the personal appearance but the good looks that go with a good speaker.
I want to say, on behalf of the good people of Niagara Falls, and they are all good people, that we do appreciate the splendid work of our Speaker when he served as a commissioner on the Rainbow bridge at Niagara Falls. He accomplished a very fine job. I should like also to congratulate the Deputy Speaker as well as the hon. member tor Spadina (Mr. Rea) on their appointments. I had the privilege of serving with the hon. member for Spadina for many years in the provincial legislature. I knew, from the experience I gained with him then, that he had many fine qualities and would some time take a prominent part in leadership in another place. I should like as well, Mr. Speaker, because it is an honoured custom, to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am not a lawyer, and I am thankful for that, but if I were a legal man I would say that these hon. members made an excellent job of a poor case.
I could not help but notice as I entered this house, and I presume most members who were here in the last parliament noticed the same thing, the many new faces we have with us. I must say they are exceptionally good-looking as well. However, it did make me feel a little at home to see the faces of those with whom I had been associated in the provincial legislature. First there was the genial member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Villeneuve). While he served as a member

The Address-Mr. Houck in Toronto he performed a major job and I realized then he was a valuable member. He served as chairman of some of the important committees and performed a splendid job.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of serving with the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett), that good-looking and most eligible bachelor in the house at the present time. I want to say to him, if it will be any incentive, that if he wants to come to Niagara Falls on his honeymoon I will see that he has the honeymoon suite at the hotel with our compliments. I served also with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Beech). I always appreciated the definite interest he took in the problems of the returned men. He did a very splendid job in that respect. Now, Mr. Speaker, perhaps to bring it a little closer home to my own party, I may say that I served also with our whip, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel), who I think is doing a splendid job as whip of this great party.
I have listened with great interest to many hon. members tell about their own ridings. What can I say about Niagara Falls? Certainly everybody in the Dominion of Canada, yes in the whole world, knows something about Niagara Falls. I would only be wasting the time of this house if I were to try to say something about the falls itself.
As I have said previously, and I say it truly again today, we are mighty proud of Niagara Falls, but in no way are we jealous or selfish in any respect. We want to share it with the rest of the world. We are, of course, known as the honeymoon centre of the world; but at the same time we do not hold ourselves responsible for some of those people who unfortunately get fed up on life, come back to the falls and use it as a jumping off place.
I know also that many hon. members, especially the new ones, are from distant places in our dominion and, because of circumstances, are forced to spend their week ends in Ottawa. I should like to say to them this morning, Mr. Speaker, and I say it sincerely indeed, that I cordially invite them to come to Niagara Falls on any week end. It is only a matter of a 12-hour trip by train. I will see to it, through our good mayor, that they will be royally treated and that the city will be at their command. If perchance they run afoul of the law and are forced to spend a few unpleasant hours in that terrible jail we have in Niagara Falls, I will gladly send them down some of the old Hansards to read so they may feel at home.
Seriously, may I say that I think they not only would enjoy themselves but that the trip would be most profitable. Not only could they

view our wonderful scenery but they could go through the new Sir Adam Beck power plant and see the new open cut hydro canal, something which would be well worth their while. I know a great many people are talking about the beauty of Niagara Falls in blossom time, but I want to assure hon. members of this house that Niagara Falls is in full dress at any time of the year. I therefore want to say again that hon. members are invited to come down and see the greatest place in the world.
I should now like to touch briefly on two matters to which I have made reference on two previous occasions. My first point is with regard to the great obstruction to automobile traffic crossing the Welland ship canal which exists at Homer, where the raising and lowering of the bridge impedes the constant flow of traffic. The condition there is greatly aggravated during the summer months by reason of the tourist traffic from the United States proceeding across the river at Fort Erie and at Niagara Falls, and the traffic proceeding from Canada into the United States.
Many and long delays occur at this point. One would not have to be an engineer to realize that a permanent cure could be effected only by building an overhead bridge or a tunnel at this point. I believe a very practical suggestion has been made, namely to permit three lanes of traffic across the bridge at busy times. This traffic could be electrically controlled. I think that procedure would avoid a great deal of the congestion at the busier ends of the bridge and would do a great deal to alleviate the trouble that exists at the present time. I have fears-and I am not alone in this respect-that a serious accident will occur at this point and that loss of life might result. I am sure something could be worked out to solve this difficulty.
By actual count, Mr. Speaker, the bridges are up one quarter of the time or 6 hours out of every 24 hours during the shipping season. This situation affects the economy of our district. It is a nuisance to our inhabitants, and it costs them real money. The local taxpayers must maintain duplicate fire fighting services on both sides of the canal, and they must maintain sewage disposal units on each side of the canal as well. I say without fear of contradiction that the bottleneck to traffic at the Homer bridge is one of the worst in our country.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not say something pertaining to this problem which has been so well discussed on previous occasions by the hon. member for Lincoln and the hon. member for Welland. I would remind the Minister of Public Works and

the Minister of Transport that last year through the ports of Niagara Falls and Fort Erie between 3,500,000 and 4,000,000 tourist permits of all classes were issued. On the 4th of July week end at Fort Erie alone, including the four days from July 1 to July 4, over 150,000 cars crossed that one bridge alone. On the 4th of July there were issued at the Fort Erie bridge alone over 13,000 tourist permits. It might be of interest to hon. members of the house to know that last year at the port of Niagara Falls, 2,214,721 cars crossed and at the Port of Fort Erie 2,108,502 cars entered Canada. We are the greatest tourist receiving centre in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and I think we deserve some consideration in that respect.
I often step into the various tourist bureaux at Niagara Falls, which are controlled by the provincial government, and they tell me that one of the complaints they receive from returning tourists-and it is one of the most serious complaints-is the tie-up at the Homer bridge and at the Burlington cut-off. I am thankful to the Minister of Public Works and glad to know, according to the Globe and Mail of this morning, that next fall that trouble will be alleviated at Burlington.
I am not exaggerating, Mr. Speaker, when I say that especially on a holiday week end -and it will be understood that when the bridge goes up for navigation, shipping has
preference over all other types of traffic__
if more than one boat goes through, if perhaps there are two or three of them, I have seen with my own eyes motor cars two abreast extending all the way from St. Catharines right through to Niagara Falls, a distance of 10 miles, waiting for the bridge to go down Certainly with the advent of the St. Lawrence seaway this congestion is going to be worse than ever.
I would therefore suggest to the minister that perhaps the most economical and surely the quickest way to alleviate the situation would be to build a tunnel under this canal. This could be done easily in the winter months, and in a comparatively short time when the canal is dewatered. 1 hope relief will be given to us in this matter. I know that clergymen, lawyers, doctors or any others who have speaking engagements either at Niagara Falls or at St. Catharines always allow at least half an hour leeway in case they are tied up at this bridge.
May I say this seriously indeed, because I know the Conservative hon. member for Lincoln is vitally interested in this matter as well as the hon. member for Welland and myself. I know it is not only our hope but it is the sincere hope and prayer of all members of this house that the hon. member for
The Address-Mr. Houck Lincoln will soon be restored to health and have the privilege of meeting with us again.
At the same time I want to pay my respects to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) for the very fine officers they have at the ports of Niagara Falls and Fort Erie. They naturally are the first people to greet tourists; and once you leave a good taste in the tourist's mouth upon his entrance to Canada he is going to carry it with him all the way through his trip. In my long years of experience in public life, Mr. Speaker, I never once have had a complaint from a tourist about being handled in the wrong way by either a customs officer or an immigration officer. I therefore think we can well be proud of these civil servants who are working at those two border points.
I well remember, when I was on the government side of the house, how the government now in power acted when they were in opposition, especially the Minister of Finance, who I thought made good speeches pertaining to the excise tax on automobiles. They were very quick indeed to complain about this tax at a time when it was a sensible measure against inflation. Now that inflation is not a serious problem I say that the special excise tax on cars is not necessary, and that it should be completely eliminated. The present government reduced the tax-and I give them credit for that action-from 10 per cent to 7 \ per cent. Now the economic situation justifies a change, and that tax should be abolished.
This step certainly would reduce the price of cars and the full reduction should be passed on to the consumer. If this were done it would save the Canadian public about $60 million a year. In the United States alone the automobile industry is at least a $50 billion industry; and proportionately, according to our size, it is in about the same position in Canada. In the United States one out of every five industries has some connection with the automobile industry, and one out of every seven employed men has something to do with this industry. We can well see what a great lift it would be to our economy if this industry could receive some assistance. Certainly the abolition of this tax would increase sales because of lower prices, which would in turn stabilize employment in the production of Canadian cars and in the sales agencies across our great dominion. As a result the treasury would benefit by higher revenues from the tax on profits of these businesses.
I think we have a lack of economic realism not only with respect to this particular tax but with respect to many others, which has

The Address-Mr. Houck had the result of slowing down business and multiplying the cost of production operating generally to the detriment of the nation's economic welfare. The very jobs of countless workers depend on the ownership of a motor vehicle. For them an excise tax on cars is almost the equivalent of a licence to work. For most city dwellers that excise tax is the near equivalent to a licence to get into the country, while for rural dwellers this tax is a near equivalent to a licence on necessary trips to the shopping centres.
I do not believe there is any virtue in a tax merely because it produces revenue, but certainly there is a fundamental virtue in a fiscal system which broadens the tax base and at the same time produces necessary revenue at lower rates. We must consider the fact that in Canada manufacturing as a whole provides well over 2 million jobs. Of this total the automobile industry provides almost 400,000, in short about one job in every ten or eleven of all the jobs in our country. This figure does not include garages, service stations and suppliers such as the textile and steel mills, tire makers, etc. So I say that in a general sense the employees of the motor car industry are recruited in two principal ways. They are hired as either skilled or unskilled persons. The unskilled workers go through the process of training and in most cases become specialists in some type of job. The skilled man is put on the type of work he does best, and remains there.
Another aspect of the motor car industry employment field worth emphasizing is the fact that the entire automobile or truck is not manufactured at the motor car plant proper. A high percentage of the content is built by smaller industrial organizations known as suppliers in widely scattered industrial towns, and it is estimated that there are several hundred such suppliers. Therefore the opportunity to link up with some phase of the motor car business is almost unlimited. Other important branches of the automotive business are the sales and service fields. Every large industrial concern has an extensive sales organization. The man who aspires to be a car salesman in all probability will find his entry into the motor car business at some city or town far from the plant. He will be an employee of some dealer or distributing branch.
Judging from the fact that there are well over 5,000 automobile dealers, 15,000 independent garages and 17,000 service stations throughout this great dominion, it is quite obvious that the sale and service of motor vehicles offers employment in a wide field of occupations, including salesmen, accountants,


partsmen, timekeepers and service manager^.
I could go on at some length, but I am urging again that this government take some recognition of these facts and completely eliminate the excise tax.
I want to say a few words now about the recession. I think one of the most remarkable factors in this recession is that the people who are employed are as reluctant about the spending of money as are those who are unemployed. Yet the people who are unemployed cannot hope to get back to work if those who are employed do not engage in purchasing. I think the psychological moment is at hand when the federal, provincial and local groups should combine their efforts to uplift our economy. There is no doubt in my mind that the consumers who have the money but not the confidence to buy should be encouraged to make home improvements and obtain the goods and services they need. Certainly if the employed people are hesitant to indulge in purchasing, more and more people will be out of work.
There is not much point in letting our nation reach a depression because so many thousands of people are out of work. It is our duty as members of this house to try to help the economy instead of permitting it to grow worse. The big battery of anti-recession proposals produced not only by the political parties but by other organizations ought to be judged at least in part by the answer to one question: how soon can these proposals be brought into effect? Certainly this government should use every incentive to spur consumers and businessmen alike to spend. This is not a matter of theory but one of economic reality. It does not matter whether we like or dislike heavy government spending; what counts is that governments cannot move quickly in actually undertaking public works. Some projects must be subject to agreement among the various levels of government; others require the acquisition of land and rights of way, or require drafting, designing and engineering. The real job-creating effects of public works projects do not appear until many, many months after the decision to go ahead has been taken.
Consumers and businessmen, on the other hand, can start spending quickly. Few households in this country exist without unfilled wants; few businesses exist where there is not some plan for growth which could be put into effect if depreciation provisions were favourable. Certainly the fundamental fact of government spending must be that it can only do a little about a recession. The real thing that counts is what people do with their money.
It is my firm belief that great assistance could be given by this government to bring

down the price of food in Canada. With 500,000 people out of work I do not see how they can pay for the food they need at present prices. During the depression of the thirties food was cheap; a person could almost live on $5 a week at that time. The situation today is different; with thousands out of work and the cost of living sky high everyone is asking the question, "When is this government going to act?"
1 would suggest this government give consideration to a gradual five year cut in corporate and individual taxes to make more money available for investment and industrial expansion. This would create a lot more jobs, and certainly millions of our dollars could be funneled into the private economy through reductions in all brackets of individual income taxes. The prescription for ending a business slump is simply to sell more goods and get production lines humming again. I think one of the basic problems facing the economy is that of moving more goods from the factory to the home. Certainly production capacity has increased at a faster pace than has consumption.
I am glad to say that industry, if I may use the vernacular, is putting the screws on its salesmen to bring consumption up to meet production. Not only automobile dealers but other industries should start going out looking for customers rather than waiting for customers to come to them. When we consider that 42 per cent of our sheet steel production goes into the automobile industry we can well see that if that business were given a lift it would indeed mean a pick up in the basic steel industry, which in turn would mean a lift to our entire economy.
We must never forget that the customer is king. Give him what he wants and needs and he will spend the money to buy it. Certainly the time has arrived when people with money in their pockets are tired of being ignored or kicked around by salesmen, and they now want to be wooed as customers. Too many of our businessmen and salesmen have grown soft and have forgotten how to sell in the post-war period when the seller was king.
There is nothing wrong with our economy that a little old fashioned selling will not correct. It is about time the fog and smoke was cleared from our minds and we realized that unemployment has been increasing while national production was decreasing. Let me repeat that if we are going to have a tax cut I think it should be one which will stimulate business and employment. No temporary cut in federal income taxes would put more money in circulation, because most people would not spend it. One of the main causes of our recession today, in my opinion, 57071-3-17	.
The Address-Mr. Houck is a buyers' strike. A general price cut would trigger consumer purchasing, which in turn would stimulate business expansion. Certainly we cannot say we are out of the woods at the present time, but it would help a great deal if business people would stop talking about their problems and get out and do a job of selling.
A tax cut would do more to strengthen our economy at this time than a spending binge that could only lead to a hangover of debt and inflation. However, a tax cut will not do the job unless it is the right kind of tax cut. It must be designed to put money in the hands of investors and job creators as well as in the hands of consumers. It will not do the job if it is used simply to provide a popular political hand-out. It can succeed in its purpose only if it is designed to stimulate more production and more jobs for the Canadian people.
I believe we should have a change in our whole national attitude and approach to this matter. Confident action is needed at the present time, not just confident talk to meet the grave challenge to economic strength and leadership. False optimism has no place in our world today. We cannot talk ourselves into a boom any more than we can talk ourselves into a bust, but we can use our heads and decide now whether the urge to buy is sound for our economy and for individuals as well as being healthy for our country.
My own suggestions for action to counteract this recession would be to first extend and permanently raise unemployment insurance benefits to make purchasing power available, to raise income tax exemptions as far as possible, to stimulate public and private construction, to increase defence spending and to eliminate the 7 j per cent federal excise tax on automobile purchases. It is useless to try to explain to the unemployed that this is a recession and not a depression. To them it is a full-fledged depression, and the most vicious thing about an economic downturn is that it feeds on itself like a snowball rolling down a hill. It is easy to stop before it gains momentum and size, but if you let it get rolling it can flatten you.
Experimenting, debating and sitting tight are forms of wishful thinking, and as dangerous as waiting for a cobra to strike. Action must be taken to apply the quickest solution possible of achievement, and that is to put money in the hands of the people who lost their purchasing power through no fault of their own. This can be done by increasing unemployment insurance payments to an amount near the breadwinner's full earnings, not just to the welfare level. Under those

The Address-Mr. Houck circumstances the extension of payments is like giving a patient half the dosage. The patient does not die and does not get well but lingers on until complications make a cure impossible. The effect of raising jobless benefits would make adequate purchasing power available to the economy. A small cut in our present income tax system is as outdated as the nickel cigar.
It would seem to me that economic justice could be better served and the problem of the unemployed better resolved if a little more attention were paid by our top government officials to their plight and their unequal battle against the ever-diminishing dollar rather than for the officials to be continually listening to the advice of our great industrialists and the so-called politicians telling them what is good for the man on the street. One has only to spend an hour or two in a supermarket and watch a harried housewife trying to stretch her fast depleting dollar to learn something that might be useful to him and to the country at large.
I wish to refer again to the remarks made by the previous speaker in this debate, a very fine lawyer from Toronto, considered one of the best criminal lawyers in the province of Ontario. I wish to remind him of the fact that the vast majority of new Canadians and representatives of various ethnic groups to whom he referred were brought to Canada by this great Liberal party.
I certainly hope when that day of days arrives which all the people in Canada are looking forward to, namely budget day, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will announce that the excise tax on automobiles has been completely eliminated. I doubt if any session of parliament has had more responsibility placed on its shoulders than has this parliament. What we its members do not only in regard to international affairs but with regard to national affairs as well will have much effect upon the lives of our people this year, next year and for generations to come. We will have to guard our freedom with all the zeal possible, and we must at all costs protect our economic stability. Much will depend on what sort of effort we put forth toward achieving these objectives.
One thing is sure, Mr. Speaker. We will have to decide whether we are going to climb the long high road to freedom or stumble down communism's dead end street. It is my sincere hope and I think the hope of all hon. members that our accomplishments here in parliament will do much to help Canada maintain its place among the nations of the world, because under 22 years of Liberal government this great dominion of ours grew to be a nation outstanding and respected by

all other nations. If we conscientiously perform the task before us we should be able to throw back our shoulders and throw out our chests with pride in satisfaction with a job well done.	.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to extend to you my heartiest congratulations on your election to the high office of Deputy Speaker, and to join with others in expressing my respect and confidence in you to handle the duties of your office fairly and justly. I also wish to extend the same sentiments to Mr. Speaker and the Clerks of this honourable assembly.
In offering my modest contribution to the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I feel obliged to extend my sincere congratulations to the mover of the address, the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). It was a pleasure to listen to the speeches of these two hon. members and to note their complete mastery of the subject matter and their knowledge of our national problems. I wish to point out the distinction the hon. member for Yukon has earned for himself by having to contest three election campaigns within a period of nine months. This experience has not been duplicated by any other hon. member of this house past or present.
Further, I cannot restrain myself from describing to this house some characteristics which distinguish and set apart the constituency of Marquette which I have the honour to represent and serve. On checking back into history I find that the first election of a member to the House of Commons from Marquette was held in 1871, a year after Manitoba joined confederation. Two gentlemen, Angus McKay and James Lunch, contested the riding each receiving 282 votes. The returning officer did not then as now have a casting vote and both contenders hightailed to Ottawa. The House of Commons after some deliberation handed the matter of representation of the riding to the commission for privileges. The commission ruled that both men should be declared elected. Both were sworn in, but by the time the technicalities were overcome the federal election of 1872 occurred so that neither took his seat in the House of Commons, nor did either gentleman run in the federal election of that year.
Marquette has another distinction, that of having the great Canadian, Sir John A. Macdonald, represent it for four years from 1878 to 1882. After suffering defeat at the hands

of the electors in Kingston Sir John A. Macdonald came to Marquette, where he received an acclamation.
Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to keep on boasting about this wonderful constituency, which claims another honour, that of having within its boundaries a summer resort second to none in Canada. I do not know how many hon. members are aware of this, but we Manitobans certainly know about it. One hundred and twenty-five miles north of the United States boundary, in the Riding Mountain chain, on a broad plateau 2,200 feet above sea level, is Clear lake, a body of water nine miles long and about two miles wide. On the southern shore of that lake nestles the townsite of Wasagaming, being the Indian word for "clear water". This summer resort, known as Clear Lake, was established by order in council in 1929 and was officially opened to the public on July 26, 1933, 25 years ago. Thus this year it is celebrating its twenty-fifth birthday with a large and very interesting program under the auspices of the local chamber of commerce.
Just to give you an idea, Mr. Speaker, of the popularity of this summer resort, 630,189 people went through its gates in 1957. Of those, 27,535 were our friends from across the border, that is American tourists, bringing along with them American dollars. The surrounding forest reserve abounds in large game such as deer, elk-as a matter of fact one of the largest herds of elk grazes on the slopes of this forest reserve-moose and bear, and there is an enclosure for buffalo which attracts a lot of visitors. The lake itself is most picturesque, and its natural attractions are supplemented by facilities for the enjoyment of outdoor life and recreation. Its buildings are designed to harmonize with the surroundings and it has unsurpassed facilities for swimming, boating, Ashing, lawn bowling and golAng. Children's playground facilities are also abundant. I therefore wish to extend an invitation to as many hon. members as could come to spend a pleasant holiday at this summer resort of Clear Lake in my riding in Manitoba. If you come once I feel sure you will have the urge to repeat your visit.
My constituency is strictly rural and cannot boast about large cities or industries, but it can boast about being the home of the best farmers in Manitoba. Oh, yes; one can meet in Marquette Canadians of many racial origins. The Arst pioneers to this riding were of Anglo-Saxon stock, and these still form the bulk of the population. Some came from the British Isles and others from Ontario, trekking into this central Manitoba woodland. They experienced the usual pioneer
57071-3-174
The Address-Mr. Mandziuk hardships, but they gave a start to and built the foundations which resulted in the present achievements in the constituency.
Next in numbers to come to my riding were the Ukrainians from south central Europe. They came in contact with Anglo-Saxons, Mr. Speaker, a people with different language, different customs, different culture and different political background. The Ukrainians had migrated to Canada in search of land, freedom and opportunity for themselves and their children. They found more than they hoped for but the adjustment to the new ways of life was long and painful. The Anglo-Saxons gave the newcomers a helping hand. With them they shared the pioneer hardships, and in spite of early suspicion of each other they soon became good neighbours and as such they became dependent upon each other.
About the same time people from other lands came into my riding, namely Frenchmen, Poles, Scandinavians and a sprinkling of every race in Europe. Each racial group at Arst tried to establish a community life of its own, Mr. Speaker; but today I am proud to say-and I speak with authority because I have lived in the pioneer period and experienced the changes in western Canada as well as in Marquette-all these people have become integrated into one Canadian community. The differences in language, customs and habits have been overcome. Suspicion of each other has melted away, and before our very eyes one can see the birth of a young Canadian race. Each race is contributing the best of its cultural riches to the altar of new Canadianism, and one sees the Canadian of the future embodying the best characteristics of each race. I am happy to note that this is evident not only in my riding but throughout Canada, Mr. Speaker.
In the meantime each racial group, while adopting the English language as the basis of common understanding, treasures its own language and customs, realizing that if they 'ose those treasures they will have nothing to place on the altar of true Canadianism. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege and an honour to represent such people.
Marquette is an agricultural constituency dotted with villages and towns whose very existence depends on the welfare of the farmer. For more reasons than one they voted for me on March 31 last. The efforts of the government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, to give the western Canadian producer a larger share.of the national income, and its performance during the last parliament proved to western Canada and to my constituents that the Progressive Conservative party keeps its election promises. During the March campaign the opposition,

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk both Liberals and Socialists, minimized the efforts of our government; but the voters on March 31 gave unqualified approval of what had been done and, by so doing, expressed confidence in our party and in our leadership. Hence a full contingent of 14 members from Manitoba are on the government side of the house.
The western farmer rejected those selfappointed champions of agriculture and industry. He rejected those who shed crocodile tears over the plight of the farmer but who strenuously opposed every measure introduced by this government for the benefit of the farmer during the short session of the twenty-third parliament. Those who fought against cash advances, those who slandered and denounced the agricultural stabilization bill, that famous Bill No. 237, received an answer to their heroic efforts at the polls on March 31. While no one interested in price supports expected that it would be a cure-all, yet most people felt that it was a step in the right direction and, under proper administration, would improve the conditions of Canadian agriculture.
Those in this house who try to perform a post mortem on why the Progressive Conservative party won such a sweeping victory at the polls on March 31 would do better to make some soul-searching reflections on why they lost the confidence of the Canadian people. Our Prime Minister, while speaking in the maritimes during the last campaign, said that in ordinary life we judge people by the way they keep their promises, and it is not any different in politics.
We listened with interest to the speech from the throne, and I feel that the proposed legislation it outlined is welcomed by the Canadian people.
We are happy to note that greater efforts are being made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to sell our agricultural and fisheries products. According to reports Canada is exporting more wheat than in the corresponding period last year while the wheat exports of our competitors have fallen off. This is an indication of good salesmanship on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It also indicates that the attendance of the Prime Minister at the London conference last June and the sending of a trade mission to Britain are paying off.
The price stabilization act passed by the last parliament and in operation since May 5 is receiving widespread approval. Setting a guaranteed price on a product enables the primary producer to plan his operations without risk of falling prices while the product is being prepared for market.
I am pleased to note, Mr. Speaker, that several amendments will be introduced to

the cash advance legislation. Although it was the best piece of legislation placed on the statute books during the last session, certain weaknesses have showed up in its operation and amendments will be welcomed. This type of legislation was asked for by the grain producers for a number of years, to which pleas the former Liberal administration turned a deaf ear. It took the Progressive Conservative party to bring it into force.
I have heard nothing but praise for it from farmers, merchants and businessmen, including bank managers. Since it went into force collections have been better. Yet, like all new legislation, weaknesses have shown up in its operation.
Among others, may I be permitted to mention the inconvenience and delay in the obtaining of a cash advance by a tenant farmer whose landlord does not reside in the district. Second, there is the inability to obtain a cash advance by the farmer who has shipped a carload of malt barley, although he has sufficient grain in storage to warrant a cash advance. Another weakness is the deduction made in the case of the farmer who delivers grain for the purchase of registered seed. I hope, therefore, these weaknesses will be taken care of by proper amendments as anticipated in the speech from the throne. I have no doubt that the Minister of Agriculture, who has this matter under consideration, will bring in such amendments.
The anticipated amendment of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act will be welcomed by the farmers of the western prairies generally, including those in my constituency. In its present form the act has proved highly unsatisfactory, and I hope the amendments will remedy the situation. I might suggest that the general feeling in the country is that this legislation should be completely rewritten or repealed in its entirety when some form of crop insurance is put in force to replace it.
Our small businessmen no doubt will welcome the idea of the establishment of a small business section within the administrative machinery of the government, as the unhealthy state of the agricultural industry has affected them no less than those upon whom they depend, the agricultural producers.
I wish to commend the government for appointing the Bracken commission to investigate the problem of box car allocation to the grain elevators of western Canada. It is hoped that the commission's findings and their implementation will remedy the grievances of the western producers.

Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with my formal remarks I should like, as all other members have done so far, to extend my personal congratulations to the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr Michener) on his unanimous election as Speaker of the House of Commons. This is an indication of our individual and personal support arising from his ability and fairness in presiding over the House of Commons.
Hon. members may recall that during the last parliament I made some reference to the office of Speaker and suggested that it should be a permanent position, as did the Prime Minister some time ago. I am still of that opinion. I believe we could quite properly adopt the proposal I made during the last parliament, that the Speaker of the House of Commons should not have to stand for election in a particular constituency but rather should be elected by the membership of the House of Commons, those members forming the constituency that he would represent. This would permit every constituency in Canada to have someone representing them sitting in the House of Commons with a voice and a vote, someone able to take part vocally in presenting their problems and ideas and to make suggestions as to solutions.
Just prior to the calling of the election in Manitoba the premier of that province made a similar proposal regarding the appointment of a permanent speaker for the legislature of that province. He also undertook to institute certain legislative changes that would be required. I hope we will undertake to do something similar so that in the years to come we may have a permanent Speaker established here as in the House of Commons in England, one who would not be connected with politics and who would be able to discharge more fairly the duties of that office.
