Mr. Speaker, it seems a rather hollow effort to be participating in this debate when there are so many empty seats. The cabinet is represented by one hon. member, but unfortunately I have no intention of dealing with the department that comes under his jurisdiction. I should like, however, to make a reference to the $1,185 million public works program which was announced during the election campaign-coincidentally during the election campaign, I might add. All I could find of this $1,185 million that will apply to
The Address-Mr. Howard the constituency of Skeena, which incidentally covers an area almost one-third the size of the entire province of British Columbia, is an item for $1.5 million for one project and some smaller amounts for other smaller projects.
I am going to suggest, therefore, that the Department of Public Works dust off some of the files that are hiding in the back rooms, and they will find countless suggestions and requests for much needed public works projects in that particular riding, ranging all the way from major items like federal buildings in the newly developed community of Kitimat and in Prince Rupert to such things as small wharves on the lakes in the interior part of the riding.
One thing that could be placed in the public works program of this federal government, and something which has been advocated by a number of people for many years as well as by the government of British Columbia, is the construction of a second trans-Canada highway. It has been advocated that the federal government and the provincial governments of the western provinces enter into an agreement for the building of such a route. This project was discussed at some length during the election. We know it was a major item in the election campaign of the Liberal party. We know also that same party, when they were in office, turned a deaf ear to the proposals for just such a second trans-Canada highway. The proposal would be on a 50-50 basis, somewhat similar to the financial agreement that exists now between the provinces and the federal government with respect to the present trans-Canada highway.
If this vision of opening up the north is to be brought to some realization this is one way in which it can be done; or this could be complementary to the opening up of the northern part of Canada. At the moment there are sections of highway along that route that have been built by provincial governments, but they are not connected and many of the portions through the central part of Canada could not be properly classed as highways at all. They are mere backwoods trails following some old logging roads built by the logging companies in that part of the country years ago. Until such time as the federal government is willing to participate with the provinces in building highways, especially cross-country highways, the possibility of developing the north is going to be hindered. I hope this government will undertake to review the position taken by the past Liberal administration with respect to these proposals, and will arrange to enter into an agreement with the provinces for the building of such a trans-Canada highway on a 50-50 basis at the earliest possible moment.

The Address-Mr. Howard All our problems are not domestic, Mr. Speaker. There are some rather serious ones in the international field. I should like to expand upon the thoughts expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Vancouver East the other day, and in doing so to deal with the question of formal and diplomatic recognition of what we call red China, the people's republic of China or the mainland colony of China, whatever you want to call it. During the last session the Southam Press conducted a poll amongst members of the house asking their opinion as to diplomatic and formal recognition of red China. The results of that poll were published in the newspapers which the Southam Press have under their jurisdiction.
Among the representatives in the present parliament who answered that poll as to whether or not we should formally recognize red China, on the Conservative side of the house I can recall that both the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Victoria expressed their agreement with the recognition of red China. The attitude of the C.C.F. is well known and has been expressed a number of times over the years. We have been in the past, and still are, in complete agreement with the formal and diplomatic recognition of China. The Leader of the Opposition while he did not express himself quite so clearly on this subject when he was the Secretary of State for External Affairs, nevertheless did express himself clearly when he was relieved of that position. If he expresses the attitude of the Liberal party, then we can logically assume that the Liberal party is in favour of extending this diplomatic recognition.
There is one group in the house, Mr. Speaker, whose attitude is not clear. The Prime Minister has placed comments on Hansard concerning the attitude of the government, but I still submit that attitude is not clear. Probably I should refer to the comments of the Prime Minister when this question was dealt with in the house in November of last year. He was answering some questions on the orders of the day and at page 654 of Hansard for November 1, 1957, he said:
The attitude of this government is unchanged in that direction,-
He was speaking of formal recognition.
-and until such time as the people's government, the communist government of China, expiates its wrongdoing under international law there certainly will be no justification for the granting of recognition as we see it.
Then of course there was some discussion and inquiry as to what the word "expiates" meant. We were told to look in the dictionary. I am going to suggest that the attitude

expressed then by the Prime Minister was nothing but mere subterfuge to cover the real reason this government refuses to take this logical and necessary step. The answer given by the Prime Minister was not the real reason. Canada's position now, as it was under the Liberal administration, is merely one of following and aping the United States, instead of taking unilateral action as the United Kingdom did some years ago.
During the election campaign the people of this country were asked to follow John-I believe that was the slogan-not realizing at the time, at least in this and other international affairs, that the John they were asked to follow was John Foster Dulles of the United States. The previous attitude of the United States government with respect to this particular issue of recognizing China diplomatically was a flat and unalterable "No; we refuse to have anything to do with it and that is that". But in recent months we find this gentleman John Foster Dulles changing his attitude just a little bit, laying the groundwork for an about face on the question of the recognition of China. Previously the answer was a flat no to any proposal for recognition. Now the attitude as expressed by that gentleman is "We will recognize red China or communist China when it is advantageous to the United States to do so". That day will not be too far distant. When it happens, with the connected question of expanded trade, Canada once again will be caught short and will be behind the eight ball in its dealings with that country.
Another reason is the attitude of the Prime Minister in saying that China must expiate its sins; and I think we can only assume that he was making reference to its attitude toward Korea during the Korean war. If we follow logically along and that is the real reason this government will not have anything to do with diplomatic recognition, then we can obviously assume that the government's attitude is that we should cut off diplomatic relations with the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics because of what that government did in Hungary not too long ago. It is precisely the same thing, where a larger nation interfered with the desires of a helpless nation and dictated to them the way they were going to operate their country. If it is for the political colour and complexion of China-with which I do not agree-then we can logically say that this government's attitude is to cut off diplomatic relations with Czechoslavakia, Yugoslavia and many other countries, including Egypt or the united Arab republic, as it is called.
Another thing that does not add up, so far as the attitude of the Prime Minister and

this government is concerned on this question of the moral necessity of diplomatically recognizing these nations, is shown very clearly in the attitude he expressed a little over a year ago with respect to a well-known individual in Egypt, as it was then, and his attitude in recent months. I do not like to make too many references to former debates as reported in Hansard, Mr. Speaker, but it is necessary to do so once in a while, as in this case. At page 801 of Hansard of January 30, 1957, the present Prime Minister who was then sitting on this side of the house as leader of the opposition said it was elevating Nasser to a prominent position as the dictator of the Middle East, and as the predeterminator, according to his will and his whim, of the orders made by the United Nations. He called him a grave wrongdoer, a person who had an attitude of international brigandage, and said he should become a law-abiding member of the United Nations.
It may be perfectly all right for the Prime Minister to have had those opinions at that time, but we discovered that this government almost fell over itself in its hurry to extend diplomatic recognition to the united Arab republic after it was formed and under the control of this same individual, to whom the Prime Minister a little over a year ago referred as a dictator, a wrongdoer and a person promoting international brigandage.
Again, I only mention this matter in order to show that the real reason this government refuses to take steps to deal with the question of recognition of China is as a result of the domination or the attitude of the United States in this matter. We have a moral obligation to recognize something that exists, something that is a fact, something that is there. It is a government that is in office. I, for instance, probably do not like the fact that they have a particular government in China any more than I like the fact that we have a particular type of government here in Canada, not that I am drawing any connection between the two as far as political philosophy is concerned. However, I am obliged to accept the fact that the government is here, that the Conservatives are sitting over there on the government side, much as I may not like it. The same gentlemen will agree with that statement, yet will refuse to agree with the fact that in China they have a particular government and that we must recognize the fact that that government is there. It is a moral obligation that we have.
There is another reason. If you do not want to live up to the moral obligations that exist, it may be that the economic question will have a bearing on it, for certainly our trade
The Address-Mr. Howard with other countries is one subject that should command the interest of everybody in this house and everybody in the nation who has the welfare of the economy of the nation at heart. In fact the subamendment that we are now discussing deals with the question of trade. The amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition also deals with the question of trade. Throughout the last election campaign numerous references were made to trading with other countries, both by government members and by members of other parties.
There seems to be an attitude that trading with a country, selling surplus goods to another country, has no connection with whether or not you give that country formal and diplomatic recognition. In fact the Prime Minister, speaking in the house last November, made reference to this matter when it was brought to his attention that the United Kingdom had recognized China in a diplomatic manner. His answer at that time was to the effect that it had not helped the United Kingdom in expanding its trade; that is to say, because the United Kingdom had recognized China it had not helped to expand the United Kingdom's trade with that country.
That, of course, as I am sure the Prime Minister knew at the time he made that statement-and if he did not know he should have known-is utter nonsense. Some statistics received from the United Kingdom information bureau here in Ottawa about the United Kingdom's trade with China show that the Prime Minister-and I will give credit where credit is due-was partially correct because during the years of the Korean war the United Kingdom's trade with China did not increase. But following that war we find that it increased by leaps and bounds during 1953, 1954, 1955 and 1956 to a point where it is more than double, and that in a five-year period since the armistice ending the Korean war. Hence when the Prime Minister said it did not help Great Britain, it was not a factual statement or a true statement; and I am sure that if he had the opportunity now, even though he is not here in the house, he would probably correct that impression. Because the United Kingdom undertook to deal in a neighbourly fashion with the Chinese government, British trade with China has been expanding by leaps and bounds ever since.
Therefore if Canada, with all the surplus lumber we have, particularly in British Columbia where probably more than half the total lumber produced in Canada originates, and with the wheat surpluses in the mid-western provinces just sitting there

The Address-Mr. Keays waiting to be moved and exported, were to treat China in a neighbourly fashion and exchange diplomats just as we have with the united Arab republic-of which we were so critical not too long ago-surely we could expect to expand our trade by selling to the more than 600 million people who live in China, thus helping to bolster our lagging economy.
In many respects there has been an unfortunate attitude on the part of the western nations which has driven China precisely where we did not want it to go, that is to say into the arms of the Soviet union. Unless we take some steps to reverse that trend our relationships with the Soviet powers are going to worsen, not from a military standpoint but from an economic standpoint, which of course is our main concern. As was expressed earlier, as sure as we are sitting here at this moment the United States will in the not too distant future do what John Foster Dulles said they would do; that is, recognize China when it is advantageous to the United States to do so, and it will be advantageous to do so pretty soon. Canada once again will find itself behind the eight ball and will suffer accordingly.
Canada can do two things in this respect; and these remarks are not confined to our relationships with China but cover the relationships between the nations of the western world. The nation of Canada has a prestige in world affairs far beyond what might be expected having regard to its size. In diplomatic affairs Canada is looked upon as being a fair and decent nation with a fair and decent attitude toward other countries, and we should use the prestige we have to promote international peace, to promote trade and to promote an understanding among the people of different countries not only with respect to our understanding of other countries but with respect to the understanding and appreciation of other countries as to what Canada is and the type of people we have in our country.
We should undertake, particularly with respect to China, to send an official group- I do not care if it is a diplomatic or parliamentary group or a delegation of some other nature-but we should send to China a group of people with some official or semi-official status so we can get a first-hand picture of what the Chinese people are like and what their requirements are, so they in turn will get an understanding of us and will find that, after all, we are human beings just as they are. Through such an interchange between groups with official or semi-official sanction we may find a way to improve relations between the countries of east and west and at
the same time assist our economy to get out of the state of doldrums in which it is at the present time, laying the groundwork for expanding our trade.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would emphasize that there are two reasons why we must take these steps. One is a moral obligation to recognize the fact that there is a need here; and if we do not accept the first reason, then there is the straight economic reason that we must expand our trade and keep our industries going.

It is my honour to represent the constituency of Westmorland which is located on the east coast of New Brunswick, immediately to the north of Cumberland county in the province of Nova Scotia. Westmorland is a very large riding, having both a rural and urban population of nearly 100,000 people and a most diversified economy. The citizens are mostly of British and French Acadian stock. In fact, the two groups are nearly equal in number.
The maritime provinces for a great many years have been looked upon by the rest of the people of Canada as a depressed area. The term "We never had it so good", never applied to New Brunswick or Westmorland constituency. It was only recently, in fact during the 23rd parliament of Canada, that recognition of our needs received long awaited federal approval. This was brought about by the fact that on June 10 last the electors of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick elected to this house in ever increasing numbers, supporters of the Progressive Conservative party. As a result of this large representation, and nothwithstanding the short life of the 23rd parliament, beneficial legislation was passed with a view to improving the present and future economic outlook for Atlantic Canada.
The legislation to which I refer is commonly known as the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants which will have the effect of increasing the provincial treasury of New Brunswick to the extent of $7.5 million for the next four years. The total in so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned will amount to $100 million during the four-year period. This aid will definitely assist our economy and it is hoped that at the end of the four-year period it will not be necessary for maritime members to urge the government to bring in further legislation by way of aid. At that time it is hoped that the average income in the province of New Brunswick will be equal to or even greater than the national average.
Many thousands of my constituents are employed by the Canadian National Railways. The city of Moncton, commonly known as the hub of the maritimes, is a fast growing community of approximately 40,000 citizens, and in it is the head office of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways. Recent layoffs by the C.N.R. in the Atlantic region and in Westmorland county in particular have caused a great deal of hardship and worry to the men affected and in no small way will contribute adversely to the economy of eastern New Brunswick.
With our pool of labour I believe it should be possible for Canadian National Railways

to build in the city of Moncton modern offices to house the regional staff and to consider forthwith and make plans for the construction of a much needed modern station and, if possible, a C.N.R. hotel. The men employed at the Canadian National Railways shops in Moncton are well trained and competent tradesmen and it should be possible for the government to urge this crown corporation to manufacture freight cars and other equipment in these shops in order to guarantee permanent work and security for the thousands now employed by the railway in eastern New Brunswick. Wooden structures and buildings erected years ago which are an eyesore to many communities should be dismantled and be replaced by modern buildings of masonry and steel.
In addition to the large numbers of railway employees I am pleased to report to you, Mr. Speaker, that many other federal agencies are located in Westmorland constituency. The maritime penitentiary, consisting of many large buildings and an ever increasing staff, is located at Dorchester which is the shire town of the county of Westmorland. The Department of Fisheries and the Department of Agriculture, both of which are beneficial to Westmorland county, each occupy space and have large staffs in the city of Moncton. There is also in this constituency the local and maritime regional offices of the unemployment insurance commission. I am also pleased to advise the house and you, Mr. Speaker, that the civil service commission maintains in the city of Moncton a regional office which services the constituency of Westmorland together with the province of New Brunswick.
In more recent years Department of Transport employees in ever increasing numbers have been employed at Lakeburn, the site of the Moncton airport. This department has been occupying rental space in the L'Assomp-tion building, together with the staff of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. You will readily appreciate that the accumulation of civil servants has greatly aided the general economy of Westmorland county, and I am pleased to extend to the ministers an invitation to increase the staffs of their respective departments so as to relocate more and more civil servants in eastern New Brunswick.
I am sure that this brief introduction of Westmorland county will help the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to appreciate the urgent need for the construction of another large public building in which to house the present government offices and to take care of the future growth and expansion of these most important federal agencies.
The Address-Mr. Creaghan
Much has been said in previous parliaments about the proposed construction of the Chi-gnecto canal. Many maritimers are of the opinion that this canal should have been built in conjunction with the St. Lawrence seaway. A canal at Chignecto would be navigable at all times. Ships travelling the seaway to South America and the United States would shorten their route by nearly 500 miles. The canal would also be of great benefit to local shipping. Its construction would do much to cure any deficiency in the maritime economy and it is certainly justified as an extension easterly of the St. Lawrence seaway. Probably the cost of construction would be less by several million dollars than the amount that the seaway has already exceeded the original estimates. I appreciate that it will take a great deal of money and planning to build the canal. I merely wanted to mention the project today, knowing that it will be discussed by others at a later date.
During the election campaign speakers, including myself, stated that the immediate construction of the Tantramar dam would be urged on this government. Tenders were called and were opened on May 14. This construction will prevent flooding from the sea of all farm land above the dam, and will give permanent protection to several thousand acres of land. This will have the effect of encouraging farmers in their work. It will also help the general economy of my riding during the construction time. In fact, the dam is needed immediately as it will act as a causeway for a small portion of the trans-Canada highway between the town of Sack-ville in Westmorland county and the town of Amherst in Nova Scotia. The specifications for this dam call for completion during the year 1959. I have been assured that the contract will be awarded in the immediate future. It would appear as if construction of the dam will commence within one month.
Much has been said since confederation about guaranteed transportation between the province of Prince Edward Island and the mainland of New Brunswick. At the present time there is an outdated link. The ferry is modern and up to standard but cannot adequately handle the road and rail traffic between the province of Prince Edward Island and Westmorland county.
I am pleased that an extensive survey was recently authorized and I know that all members of this house would join with the four hon. members from the province of Prince Edward Island in urging this government to proceed with the New Bruns-wick-Prince Edward Island causeway immediately the Department of Public Works is in receipt of a favourable report. The Minister of Public Works and the Minister
272	MOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Creaghan of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) have already shown keen interest in this causeway and as the approach to the causeway will be from the shore of Westmorland county many of my constituents are very interested in this scheme and, like myself, are anxiously awaiting its completion.
The decentralization of the huge national defence expenditure will also greatly help the maritimes. No. 5 supply depot, Royal Canadian Air Force, is located in various localities in Westmorland. The buildings were in most cases erected during the last war and have given good service. I hope during the course of this parliament that the base will be enlarged and that permanent and modern military buildings will be erected. I also urge the government and the Department of National Defence in particular to consider an even more important role for the huge army camp at Gagetown.
It is most difficult to mention all the needs of my constituents in this my first speech. As in the areas represented by many other members we have many farmers in Westmorland county who have problems requiring immediate attention at Ottawa. Many of these farmers have negotiated mortgages through the Canadian farm loan board but unlike the western farmers many of our farmers are part-time farmers. It would be of great assistance if the legislation could be amended to permit them to become eligible applicants under the Canadian farm loan board jurisdiction. This would eventually create more full-time farmers in New Brunswick and would encourage improvements in the area.
Like the areas represented by western members, my area contains great fishing industries. Westmorland has many miles of coastline and many of my electors feel that wharf construction was badly neglected in past years. The Minister of Fisheries is well aware of the needs of the fishermen on Northumberland strait and already much has been done by him during his short term of office. Recent estimates of the Department of Public Works provide more generous assistance for the construction of wharves in New Brunswick.
I hope that hon. members will not get the impression that I have come to Ottawa with a chip on my shoulder or as a prejudiced maritimer. I represent a seat which invariably elected a supporter of the Liberal party. This pattern has been a continuous one since the election of 1935, notwithstanding the serious state of affairs I have mentioned today. I hope that at the end of this parliament and that, as a result of action the previous election trend will be reversed.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate you on your appointment to the speakership of the house. I have known you for a number of years and I am well acquainted with your sense of justice and your impartiality. I can say that I was deeply appreciative of your appointment.
I congratulate also the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) on his appointment to the deputy speakership. We know that he is the descendant of a noble line of ancestors who have left their mark on the house. Knowing his talents, we can be assured that his term of office will be rewarding. I want to express to him every good wish in this connection.
Mr. Speaker, I also would like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the magnificent way in which they have acquitted themselves of their task.
I would not like either to omit mentioning the appointment of the hon. members for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) to their respective functions of Minister of Defence Production and of Secretary of State. All of us know the energy and the qualifications of both those gallant members who have become ministers of the Crown. We believe and hope that their energy and their talents will be used to promote the welfare of all their Canadian fellow-citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to thank the electors of the constituency of Papineau whom I represent in this house for the third time. I thank them for this mark of esteem and appreciation which they have given me by electing me again. I can assure them that I will always serve them with loyalty and devotion and that I will protect their interests together with those of the Canadian nation.
The speech from the throne announces some steps to alleviate the present problem of unemployment. It announces a program of public works as well as amendments to the National Housing Act and to the Unemployment Insurance Act. These measures will not be sufficient to cure unemployment, as they are but a temporary remedy. However, I say this incidentally, without such measures our economy would fall into chaos, and we would be back to the years 1930-35.
The social security legislation, that is the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, the

Disabled Persons Act and the Blind Persons Act, initiated by the Liberal party, support in some measure the purchasing power of the population and save our people from poverty and want. There is deep uneasiness in the country and the government does not seem to realize it. On the one hand, we have a great number of unemployed and, on the other hand, the cost of living continues to rise. What does the government propose to do to remedy that situation? We see nothing in the speech from the throne to lead us to expect a solution to this state of affairs. We believe that the government will finally have to follow the example of the United States where the economy suffers from the same evil as ours and where a senate committee recently recommended that salaries and prices be frozen at their present levels.
Amendments to the National Housing Act will not solve the unemployment problem because houses built with the money we voted are beyond the reach of three quarters of the wage earners. Moreover, in Montreal, the metropolis of our country, builders are slowing down their undertakings because they have trouble finding buyers for their houses or even tenants at the rentals they have to ask because of building costs. I also wish to mention incidentally that the price of available building lots doubled since 1953, so that housebuilding is becoming too costly and the small wage earner cannot afford to own his home.
Labour unions are claiming higher wages for men in the building trades and no one knows where those requests will end unlp^ the government sees to it and freezes salaries at present levels.
However, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me there is a remedy for the province of Quebec which would reduce unemployment, at least temporarily, as it would put some money in the taxpayer's pockets. This remedy consists merely in taking out of the coffers of the federal government the money that is kept there at the disposal of the province of Quebec and which its dictator, Mr. Duplessis, a friend of the Conservative members from Quebec in this house, never wanted to accept under the pretense of preserving autonomy. Incidentally, may I say to my Conservative colleagues from the province of Quebec that they have shown little gratitude and loyalty toward their provincial leader. A number of those who have spoken in this house have congratulated the Prime Minister of the country, that is to say their leader here, on his brilliant victory, forgetting meanwhile to thank their Quebec chief for having taken part in the victory they gained on March 31
The Address-Mr. Meiunier last. In those elections we saw the high powered Union Nationale machine in action in our constituencies, we heard promises of bits of roads and bridges, we saw money flowing all around. We even saw employees of the provincial government do their bit by working in close co-operation with Conservative candidates. And we do know that some Conservative candidates were chosen in the office of the premier of Quebec himself.
Since my Conservative colleagues do not dare praise their provincial leader publicly, but prefer to have very close private relations with him, they could possibly convince him that he could help the people of Quebec by finding work for them.
I believe that the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) who is looking at me at this time could be a good agent to negotiate with the Premier of Quebec and to come and collect here for the benefit of that province, the money at present held for it in the federal coffers.
These gentlemen might possibly convince Mr. Duplessis to accept some 50 million dollars from Ottawa for the Trans-Canada highway. Mr. Duplessis might well put aside his false sense of autonomy and, for once in his life, call for tenders for the undertaking of this work and comply with federal standards required for the inspection of work, more particularly with reference to the thickness of asphalt surfacing. But Ottawa has always been for Mr. Duplessis the capital of a foreign country and it is only since the Conservative party has come into power that he has found out that it actually is the capital of his country.
My Conservative friends could also convince Mr. Duplessis privately that he should accept university grants so that these institutions could embark on some undertakings and achieve their objectives.
Everybody knows, and the Conservative members of the province of Quebec as well as anybody else, that the universities of Laval, McGill and Montreal have deficits, that tuition fees are high and that the university is now open only to the well-to-do.
Some will possibly say that the province of Quebec is not in a position to accept those grants to universities, because those grants represent an infringement in the field of education which is a provincial responsibility. In that case, how is it that the province of Quebec has been accepting federal money for vocational and technical training, with regard to the construction of vocational schools? And this has been going on since 1937.
With reference to these university grants, may I ask if the federal government intends

The Address-Mr. Meunier to impose curricula, or if these grants are not granted unconditionally? These grants are granted by the present government, with no strings attached, and the Conservative members for Quebec especially, should attempt to find some formula which would bring our universities out of the stagnation and uncertainty in which they are plunged at this time, since the Conservative government, of which they are a part, does not seem to have any wish to change what has already been done.
Another way in which my Conservative friends from Quebec could use their influence with the present leader of the government, as well as the good offices of Mr. Duplessis, would be to see to the implementation of what they have preached during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958, and that is to reduce the aid which the government gives to underdeveloped countries under the Colombo plan. You will remember that over the last two election campaigns, you as well as other Conservative speakers have claimed that the Liberals gave money to underdeveloped countries, to foreign countries, and that Mr. Duplessis, at that time used the slogan "Duplessis gives to his province and the Liberals give to foreigners".
It is time, now that you have a majority in this house, that you put an end to this state of affairs instituted by the Liberal party, continued by the Conservative party and in which the contribution has been raised at the beginning of this year by the present government. You cannot ignore what you have preached as a means of stirring the Quebec population and I repeat that now is the time for you to do something in line with what you have said.
If contributions to the Colombo plan were too high, if you preached that we should not help underdeveloped countries, now is the time for you, the Conservative members from Quebec, to raise your voice in this house in order that your stand be known and that we should see whether you are going to support the theory you preached in the province of Quebec.
Health insurance is another field in which you could put your efforts to good effect to convince your Quebec leader. Mr. Duplessis said time and time again that he would agree to health insurance as long as the constitution was respected, and his province given its due. Your leader, Mr. Duplessis, always accused the Ottawa government under Mr. King and Mr. St. Laurent of spoliation and usurpation and it is only since June, 1957, that his voice is no longer heard on this point.

Well I think it is time that Conservative members do something to give effect to all the suggestions I made. This would give millions to the province of Quebec, millions of which the province has been deprived for several years. And, now that you are in sufficient numbers in this house, it is up to you to find a solution to the problems outlined so that Quebec may benefit from its share of the federal treasury.
I regret that there is no reference in the speech from the throne to federal-provincial financial relations because, there again, Conservative members from Quebec would have had a fine opportunity to give back to the province of Quebec what was taken from her according to Premier Duplessis. When Premier Duplessis accepted equalization payments in 1956, he stated that the province of Quebec was given only part of the money that was taken from her, but that he would be satisfied when Ottawa returns to the province of Quebec the taxation rights that were taken away from her. Premier Duplessis never understood, under a Liberal regime, that the federal government and the provinces have concurrent rights in matters of direct taxation but, now that the Conservative party is in power, he seems to have changed his understanding and his views on provincial autonomy are more restricted.
He never realized that the equalization formulas help distribute the national wealth all over the country and give a chance to the poorer provinces. He has always preferred to indulge in petty politics instead of behaving as a true Canadian concerned about the interests of our country.
I am now going to deal with another item close to the heart of Quebec Conservatives, an item for which they campaigned vehemently during the last election and of which not a word has been spoken since they are in this house. I refer to the matter of an ambassador to the Vatican. They charged the Liberals with doing nothing, and if I raise the matter, Mr. Speaker, it is because Conservative members themselves have raised it. That does not mean that I agree with them, for they have accused the Liberals of having done nothing in this respect. They did this without a full knowledge of the question and without wondering whether such an appointment would be welcomed by the religious authorities of the country or of their province. For them that matter was nothing more than an electoral platform to arouse the people, and now that they can implement what they have advocated, they consider the matter as a dead issue.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will say to my Conservative friends from Quebec that they must clearly state whether they agree with the doctrine of the Conservative party to which they belong, or whether they follow the doctrine advocated for many years by their provincial leader. To be consistent, they should dissociate themselves from their party if they object to the policies of the present government, which adheres to the main points of the Liberal administration policy and has not yet disavowed any of their laws including, as I have mentioned before, social measures like the assistance to under-developed countries, assistance to universities, federal-provincial relations and health insurance. All those acts and measures passed by the Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, have contributed to the prosperity we have known in this country until June, 1957. Those acts and measures have been enacted for the people of Canada from coast to coast and have been enforced on the same basis everywhere.
Now that I have raised those matters, which are all in direct relation with the province of Quebec, I would ask the Conservative members from Quebec, of whom we have only heard a few so far, to state what policy they intend to follow about the matters I have raised.
Mr. Speaker, I also express the wish that the present government will follow in the footsteps of the Liberal administration, so as to maintain in this country national unity of which the right hon. Louis St. Laurent has been a great champion and upholder both in word and deed. He spared no effort to prove to the Canadian nation that two great races and cultures could live together in Canada in understanding and harmony.
I hope that all the members of this house will be inspired by the ideal which has been the guiding principle of that great Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, sincere and deepest gratitude impels me to say to the electors of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere how thankful I am to them for the confidence they showed me at the election of March 31st last. They can be sure that I will devote all my energy on their behalf so that, as all the other citizens of Canada, they may enjoy the blessings of a sound Conservative administration.
Honour to whom honour is due; I interpret, here, Mr. Speaker, the feelings of my electors in congratulating you for the mark of unanimous confidence given you by this house
The Address-Mr. Paul when you were again elected as its Speaker. No doubt your experience will permit you to direct proceedings of this house even more efficiently. No doubt, in your paternal kindness, you will forgive us the few mistakes which new members like myself are bound to make.
I extend my most sincere congratulations to the hon. members for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) and Spadina (Mr. Rea) who have been chosen respectively Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman of committees of the whole.
The hon. members for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) have been entrusted with portfolios and we know, there again, that their experience, their devotion to duty and their sense of responsibility will help the government in its efforts to solve the serious problems which now face all Canadian taxpayers.
When we read in the newspapers that the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne would be the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere), the electors of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere felt deeply honoured, since the hon. member is an excellent citizen of the parish of Maskinonge; and those who had placed their legitimate hopes in him were rewarded by the tact and the eloquence with which he has delivered his speech.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) also deserves congratulations for affording us the opportunity of getting to know a part of our country about which we had been unfamiliar, and he has also helped us gain a better insight into the great projects which the government is contemplating for that area of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, other hon. members have referred to a problem which I have much at heart, as a representative of an industrious working class. I should like to touch briefly upon the textile and knitting industries.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) as well as several other members referred to the textile problem. You will permit me to associate with this problem that of the knitting industry which I consider equal in importance to the cotton industry, to the wool industry and to the dressmaking industry. In the constituency of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere, there are 5,000 workers, men and women, who earn their living in those plants. It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) whom we heard yesterday, blamed the Conservative party for this recession in the textile industry and knitting mills. On the contrary, Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Paul Speaker, this situation has prevailed in our province and in the province of Ontario since 1953, as well as in the riding of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, and, more particularly at Louiseville and St. Gabriel of Brandon where staff reduction was 18 per cent from 1953 to December, 1956. When quoting these figures yesterday, the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska was not fair to this government, because our workers at home are confident that Conservative policy will solve the problem now obtaining in the textile industry and in the knitting mills, in order to give the men and women in those plants greater prosperity and a little more work.
I know that the problem deserves attention and I am sure that the hon. ministers of trade and commerce and of finance (Mr. Churchill and Mr. Fleming) will seek an early solution taking into account, however, the difficulties of free trade with some countries like China, Japan, the United States and India.
It is a mistake to hold the Conservative party responsible for this situation in the textile industry when it is well known that, from 1935 until last year, the Liberal party was in power and did absolutely nothing to stop that depression which could be seen coming. Furthermore, for years goods prefabricated at a lower cost than that which our manufacturers have to pay on the market to sell their products before processing were allowed to come into Canada.
I know that the right hon. Prime Minister last fall asked the tariff board to review, if possible, the matter of custom tariffs so that this essential industry, the second largest in the province of Quebec, can recover the confidence it lost as a result of the Liberal party's inertia, lack of vision and of sound management.
Another matter with which I wish to deal very briefly has to do with agriculture. I deem it a duty to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) as well as the members of the 23rd parliament who enacted the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act. Why? Because through this legislation, the Canadian people, particularly the agricultural community, is in a position to enjoy an expansion and a prosperity such as they never knew under a Liberal administration. If farmers are now somewhat more prosperous, it is due to the sound administration of the government under the leadership of the Prime Minister seconded by the cabinet and particularly, in matters of agriculture, by the Minister of Agriculture.
A moment ago, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) asked

whether the Conservative party had ever enacted a truly social measure to help our farmers. I don't know that any finer legislation has ever been passed to help solve the problems of agriculture, not only in western Canada, but in the whole of this country, particularly to protect the farmers of eastern Canada. Hon. members of the opposition are a bit confused. They wonder why it is that they, who held power for 22 years, should now have to go through the cold region of opposition to refresh their memory and remember that they allowed themselves to drift away from the people, that they mocked the people and refused to give the people what it had the right to expect from them. They now attempt to make provincial politics here in the House of Commons; they seek to blame the premier of the province of Quebec for the failure of the provincial Liberal party. Well, the fact of the matter is that the federal Liberal party in the province of Quebec always sought to monopolize power through sentimentality, and succeeded in doing so, especially in 1949. Last March, the people recognized that the Conservative party was blessed with an innate sense of administration. The same thing happened in June, 1957, and today it is the federal Liberal party which has to sit in opposition. We who have been elected are pleased to encourage this opposition party so that it can fulfil its role bravely for a great many years to come.
Steps have already been taken to support agricultural prices. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to carry out the necessary investigations so that certain agricultural products, which can be found in abundance in my own constituency, may be protected by a support price in order that those who carry out certain types of farming may henceforth obtain the return they deserve. I refer at this time to tobacco and potato farming.
No doubt the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) who mentioned yesterday the cancellation of subsidies for the purchase of aluminum buckets for the maple sugar industry, had forgotten that this happened in 1954 while the Liberals were in power.
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity of asking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to set, if possible, a base price on maple products so that the maple industry, whose importance cannot be questioned and which enjoys a certain degree of prosperity may bring to the producers higher returns than it does now.

In addition, the Department of Agriculture might perhaps at some time consider the advisability of subsidizing the agricultural community in order to facilitate the purchase of fertilizers.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is necessary to amend the Farm Loans Act. It has been said about this act, and rightly so, that no loans are made under it. The members of the opposition have enacted that legislation without taking into account the needs of the farmers and the economic situation of our country. Well, it is to be hoped that this government, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture, will see to it that the interest rate on loans is lowered and the terms for obtaining these loans eased as far as possible, so that the farmers may benefit from this legislation and our agricultural class throughout the country may survive.
It was stated in the speech from the throne that we shall be called upon to consider legislation to check the plague of unemployment, that unfortunate legacy left to the Conservatives by the Liberals on the morrow of their defeat of June 10. May I be allowed, in the name of the workers in my riding, to thank the government, and more particularly the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), for having kindly considered their position when amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, and extending the additional benefit period by another six weeks. There is no doubt that this social security legislation would give our workmen not only enough money to meet the difficulties with which they have to cope, but also some hope of a better and more prosperous future.
Yesterday, I listened to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), in a splendid outbreak of oratory, request grants for his constituency. The situation which he described must have grown overnight like a toadstool since, before the present government took power, those problems did not exist, the municipalities were not in need, needed no grants, could do without federal help. That, at least, is what the hon. member for Hull would have had us understand yesterday. He asked for an interprovincial bridge for his constituency. I congratulate him on that score and I hope that the chilly atmosphere of opposition will help him understand that he, and other members of the Liberal opposition, have possibly not worked in the best interest of those they represent in the 22 years their party was in power.
The problems facing the municipalities are not new and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) will no doubt allow me to remind him of the urgent needs of my home
The Address-Mr. Paul town of Louiseville as well as those of Berthierville, of St. Gabriel de Brandon and of many other municipalities of my fine constituency, which are faced with the necessity of building sewers, waterworks and public buildings. I am convinced that the hon. Minister of Public Works will see that works of this description will be carried out not only to relieve unemployment but to help municipalities out of their present difficulties. Why? Because they have not always been treated as they should have been, especially by the Liberal party which was in power far too long.

speechtext:
Autonomy? If you will allow me, I will deal with that in a few moments and it will then be a pleasure for me to answer my hon. friend. I hope that he might get to understand it as we do in our province.
Autonomy is a matter of the deepest interest to members of the opposition. I believe that this matter of autonomy would be a perfectly chosen ground for those who would like to encourage the poor Liberal provincial opposition, now faced with the crucial problem, that of choosing itself a leader on May 31 next.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the Minister of Public Works, I appeal for his financial support so that municipal and school authorities can obtain the money which would allow them to face and solve their problems. I would like also to suggest to the minister that it is time for the government to pay real estate tax to municipalities, just as every other taxpayer does. This contribution to the needs of school and municipal administration might make it possible for these corporations to obtain revenue and to lighten the load for their own taxpayers.
At the very beginning of the session, while I was still somewhat impressed by the grandeur of the ceremonies that were going on,
I heard the voice of experience, that of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who said, and I quote from the English translation of his speech as recorded on page 54 of Hansard:
I have stated before and keep on stating that there are deep doctrinal differences between the Conservatives of the province of Quebec and those of the rest of Canada. Indeed there are in the house at this time many Conservative members from Quebec who, up to now, have spent their political career waging war against the federal government-

The Address-Mr. Paul
And in the following paragraph, we read:
One of the most interesting aspects of the last federal elections is the fact that from now on these self-styled nationalist Conservatives from Quebec will have to share the responsibilities of power with the Conservatives of the other provinces and either accept the government's policy or break with their own party.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if there is one group of people truly in a position to understand the real aspirations of the people of Quebec, it is indeed ourselves, the members from that province, who were born there and who have lived there.
The hon. member for Laurier should not be surprised at the attitude the Conservatives are going to take in the present parliament. Quebec Conservatives have never been against the federal government. Quebec Conservatives have stood against the centralization efforts of the federal Liberal party, and their position has always been consistent with the aspirations and needs, as well as the mentality of our electors. The hon. member for Laurier can rest assured that the province of Quebec trusts in the future and that may be the main reason for the sweeping defeat experienced by the Liberal party in my province at the last election.
I stated from the start that while in 1957 the province of Quebec voted in accordance with a parochial mentality, this year it was part of the tide that swept across the country and gave its confidence to the government so brilliantly led by the Prime Minister. If the province of Quebec sent 50 of us to this house, it is because it felt certain that the present government was able to act in accordance with the provisions of the constitutional act of 1867 which gave the provinces the right of direct taxation, and the federal government the right of indirect taxation.
I cannot agree with my hon. friend from St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) who said that we, in the province of Quebec, have always been against the equalization system. On the contrary, we have always felt a keen desire to see the rights of all and everyone respected as we, ourselves, in the province of Quebec, take pride in respecting the rights of minorities and of everyone around us.
The Prime Minister said in this house on November 19, 1957 that the provinces would be stating their views to the central administration, and that the central government would not impose its terms to the provinces. There, Mr. Speaker, is the explanation of the vote given in my province during the last federal election.

We are not against federalism. Our attitude will always be in conformity with that of the government, because our leader, as he has already stated and shown by his actions, intends to respect the constitutional rights guaranteed to every province. That is why, at the elections of March 31 last, the Canadian people found in our government so brilliantly led by the Prime Minister a government capable of giving each and everyone its fair share.
I noticed that my hon. friends opposite were a little surprised, bewildered, disorganized and disheartened by having to sit on the opposition side; I heard them trying to explain to the house their poor showing in the province of Quebec in the last election. They would like people to believe that those who were elected on the Conservative ticket were the instruments, the favourites, the wards of the Union Nationale government. However, the Liberal party did not fare any better in the other provinces since it could not salvage a single seat in all the western provinces. Thus, this situation is not peculiar to the province of Quebec.
It is unfortunate that some members from my province do try to disparage our administration. This is not the place for provincial politics. We are in the House of Commons and our first duty is to deal with federal politics and not to try, in this house, to alleviate the setbacks suffered in the provincial field. We are, here, in the national living-room and it is imperative that we should share in fashioning the heart and soul of our nation. We must not sacrifice three centuries of our history on the altar of popular prejudices; we have no right to discredit those who bear the same names as we do, since we are not French Canadians nor English Canadians but simply Canadians. It is the solemn duty of each and everyone of us, in our respective constituencies from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to be Canadians. Why? Because it is through the understanding between two different races, between different mentalities, different origins, different aspirations, different achievements and different languages that we shall build a great country where life will be worth living. When we answer to our electors for our mandate they will say that we have efficiently contributed to national unity. We shall have the satisfaction of having contributed to the greatness of our country. And, tomorrow when we are gone, those who come after us will have the satisfaction of seeing an ever richer harvest waving over our graves. Why? Because our country will continue its forward march towards progress, prosperity and national unity. Thank you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate you. I am very happy over your appointment to your important position which you fill with so much distinction. I also wish to congratulate the new ministers and wish them all possible success in their new duties. I also have the pleasure to congratulate the new Deputy Speaker (Mr. Sevigny) as well as the deputy chairman of committees (Mr. Rea) and to extend my best wishes to them.
I would feel remiss in my duty if I did not also mention the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Lafreniere and Mr. Nielsen), who did so well in the task entrusted to them.
(Text):
As most of the members of the house on the other side do not understand the French language, I will proceed in the English language so that I may be understood by every member. Canada being a bilingual country, and as a blending of both languages helps to enrich our Canadian culture, I should hope that some day all members of this house will learn to speak both languages. There is a decided advantage in having a knowledge of both languages. For one thing, it broadens the mind. If some day soon we should have simultaneous translation in this house, I am sure that all my colleagues as well as myself would greatly benefit from this innovation.
At this point I should like to thank my electors of Outremont-St. Jean for the confidence they have shown me by electing me for a fourth term to this house. I can assure them that I very much appreciate what they have done and that they can count on me at all times to do whatever can be done to help my constituency and the whole of Canada.
We have heard a great deal about unemployment. We hear that there are 300,000,
400,000	or 500,000 unemployed. But on Saturday this week I looked at the Gazette, a newspaper published in Montreal, and there I counted 90 notices of bailiffs' sales. That is a true barometer of the situation that exists with regard to unemployment. You can mention figures; you can do whatever you like, but in bailiffs' sales there is a story of misery and hardship. What an ordeal it is to go through. What a bitter cup it is for a married couple who have lived together, say for 35 or 40 years, to find themselves all of
The Address-Mr. Bourque a sudden dispossessed of all the things they have worked for throughout a whole lifetime.
There is one thing that I should like to say which is extremely important at the present time. Men who are 20, 21, 22, 23 years of age or possibly men up to 40 years of age may be temporarily out of work but eventually they get back to a job. But, did you ever think of the misery of the man who has worked for 25 years or 30 years for the one firm and who has been a wonderful employee, yet they reluctantly are obliged to let him go because there is no more work for him in the plant where he is employed? Do you realize that this man will possibly never be able to get a steady job again? Do you realize that this is a man who has been a staunch citizen of Canada, one who has paid his taxes regularly? Imagine the despair and the anguish of this man because he never again will be able to take his place in society.	.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) assure us that things are getting better in Canada. I wonder what these citizens whose goods and chattels have just been sold by a bailiff think about the situation in Canada and whether they think it is getting better. It is they who are suffering, not the two ministers I have just mentioned. I hope that the government will soon take the measures necessary to alleviate the suffering that exists at the present time. To this effect may I remind the Prime Minister of one of his promises. In the Gazette of February 19, 1958 he was stated to have said as follows:
"As long as I'm Prime Minister of Canada everything that can be done-everything without regard to limit-will be done to the end that no one will suffer."
The Prime Minister now has a wonderful opportunity to demonstrate his sincerity and that when he uttered those words he meant what he said.
What a wonderful difference there is between sitting in the opposition and being a member of the government. As I sat on the other side of the house for many years I listened time and again to my friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) continually protesting about the delivery of the mail once a day instead of twice. According to him the Liberals were perpetrating the greatest injustice and visiting a real hardship upon the citizens of Canada by leaving the

The Address-Mr. Bourque mail delivery at one a day. Now that he is Postmaster General we hear no more from him.
He now seems to think that one delivery of mail a day is good enough for the Canadian public. He does not now consider that one delivery of mail a day is a hardship. He could very easily remedy the situation now that he has come up to the position he occupies at the present time but he does nothing about it. When he was on this side of the house he protested continually about the many thefts that were taking place in the post offices throughout the country. These thefts still go on just the same and he seems to do nothing about the matter. Possibly he tries but he cannot do anything about it. If we look at all the bank robberies that are going on throughout Canada today we realize that it has become almost an impossibility to check them.
I should now like to mention the promises of The Prime Minister during the election campaign. Every day as the campaign went on he was raising the ante. One day in the province of Quebec he would promise one thing, then he would go to New Brunswick and promise something else. Then he would travel to Toronto and promise something entirely different from what he had promised previously. It is easy to promise anything and everything but it is not always so easy to fulfil one's promises.
The government can distribute only what it receives. The taxpayers pay the shot. There is nothing free in this world; everything must be paid for. The Prime Minister might have been sincere when he made these promises but certainly he had not given the mathematical attention he should have given to the revenues of this country, and the citizens of Canada may well find that promises made in the heat of an election campaign and not based on the revenue may prove extremely costly to them if they are implemented. I do not intend to dwell any further on this subject. Suffice it to say that I do not believe it is possible to implement all the promises made. I leave to the Prime Minister the task of again facing the citizens of Canada when he is obliged to account to them for his stewardship if he has not been able to keep faith with them. That punishment will be sufficient in itself.
The government can distribute and spend only the money it receives from taxation and duties. It may for a short time spend $1.50

where it receives only $1, but there is the inevitable end when credit stops. A man may have very good credit, he may up until now have met all his obligations, but if he starts spending $1.25 when he is receiving only $1 it will not be long before he is bankrupt. The same applies to Canada or to any other country. One must stay within the limits of the revenue he receives or he will face bankruptcy at some time.
The poor citizens who took at their face value the promises made will no doubt find themselves saddled with heavier taxes. The Prime Minister would be well advised to give serious consideration to the planning of Canada's economy. I can assure him that we on this side of the house will always be ready to approve any good measures brought forward by his government; he will find us always constructive, not destructive.
I would like at this time to mention something about which I feel something should be said. I do not remember whether this matter has been mentioned before in this house. I refer to the hoodwinking of the public by the advertising of certain companies with respect to their products. To take an example, one might buy a It-foot high by about 1 foot wide package containing a certain ingredient, but when it is opened there will be found inside about one-third ingredient and the remainder stuffed with all kinds of other goods which one did not intend to buy. I think the government should put through some legislation to ensure that when going to a store to buy oatmeal one will get oatmeal. If this practice continues for many years we will have a state of inflation because people will be buying all kinds of things they neither need nor have the money to buy.
There is another aspect of this same matter which concerns the carrying in stores of certain goods packaged and priced at 90 cents less 20 cents, special offer. This cannot be a special offer because the packages are already printed and bear the label "20 cents special offer." A genuine deal is one where merchandise is worth 90 cents and the dealer decides to make a sale for 70 cents, but if the goods are marked 90 cents and advertise this special offer of 20 cents, then somebody is getting gypped because the goods are worth only 70 cents or they would sell and would continue to sell at the higher price. I think the poor working man who is already suffering sufficient hard-

ship should be protected. He is being given the illusion of getting something for nothing while he is really paying the full price for everything he gets.
I would like now to speak about an entirely different subject, namely goof balls. I notice some hon. members are laughing but they will not be laughing in a moment. This is the first step to drug addiction. I could name many young boys of 12, 14, 15 and 18 years of age who are already drug addicts, boys who were introduced to this sort of thing by purchasing a goof ball in a confectionery store, ice cream parlour or some other place. This is a menace to the youth of our country and unless something is done immediately we will And ourselves with thousands of young addicts. I am convinced that special legislation should be passed so that this abominable practice which threatens the future of our nation and the welfare of our children will cease.
Goof balls consist of barbiturates or tranquilizer pills which, when dropped in certain liquids, have a counter effect to the purpose for which they are sold. These dope pills are possibly worth 2 cents but the boys are offered these pills, dropped into liquid, at a price of 25 cents. They get used to them and within four or five weeks find they must have them. They are completely changed and boys who have been very good at school hitherto within the short space of four or five weeks become real demons.
Many people may doubt that I am telling the truth but I happen to be the mayor of a city which has been victimized by these goof balls. I have a report in my hand six pages long from the director of the police department giving me the names, addresses and parents of children involved and the places where these pills are procurable. They are, as I have said, sold in ice cream parlours, dance halls and restaurants and have even invaded our schools. Boys are given such things in the first instance and eventually learn their disastrous effects.
This is the first step toward becoming a drug addict; the next thing is marijuana and they go to stronger drugs until they eventually become incurable. These tranquillizers or barbituate pills do not come under the drug and narcotics legislation and for that reason the Royal Canadian Mounted Police criminal investigation branch are powerless to deal with the problem. The matter rests with
The Address-Mr. Nugent the food and drug department of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the officials concerned can prosecute only if they can locate from whence the pills come and then only for sales without a licence.
There are boys and girls who simply started to buy 25 cents worth of these goof balls but on the Sunday following their first purchase they go to the ice cream parlour or some other place and the server, clerk or girl behind the counter says, "Well, you can have a goof ball today but we do not have a supply so it will be 60 cents". So they pay 60 cents and the next Sunday it is $1. These boys and girls have to steal in order to get these drugs eventually and I believe the government should do everything in its power to find out everything it can about this menace and to take steps immediately to arrest the development in this field before it gets to a point where it cannot be controlled. I say this particularly because it is a very very profitable business and wherever there is great profit there will always be some individual who will take advantage of the young or anyone else. I sincerely hope the government will be able to introduce measures to put a stop to this new threat to the youth of our country.
