speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a new member I have hesitated to rise in this house for I have always believed that I should follow the advice of my father who advised me that I should never speak until I knew what I was talking about. It has become obvious to me during the brief time in which I have sat in this house that I have much to learn before I can be of much assistance in respect of the many and varied problems concerned in the administration of our country.
I should add with respect to the question of when to speak that I have had much advice from senior and more experienced members. I have been advised that this house has not been waiting with bated breath for me to come and solve all of Canada's problems. In fact it has been rather bluntly, I thought, pointed out that if I am of any help just now it will likely be only by giving this house some impressions of my constituency of Edmonton-Strathcona and then from the standpoint of an ordinary citizen who has not yet attained the skill of experienced parliamentarians such as I have seen and heard in this house so far. I think I would do best just to follow that advice rather than my own whim in talking as I would like.
My constituency in Alberta comprises all that part of the city of Edmonton which lies

The Address-Mr. Nugent to the south of the North Saskatchewan river as well as that part of the city which takes in a good many miles of the surrounding countryside which includes some excellent farm land. The richness of the farm land in that part of the country is almost legendary and the farmers in my constituency are so industrious that their production always adds to our surplus problem even though they diversify their production with a remarkably astute eye for the markets. The land is rich all the way down and not just on the surface.
For years we have had in that area domestic coal mines and there is still much coal underground suitable for domestic fuel purposes. I should add that having been raised in a coal-mining family and having worked underground myself in coal mines to some extent I am not at all anxious to see my people forced to earn a living in such a manner as long as there are other means by which gainful endeavour can open up to them a better way of life. It is my belief that the coal now left underground may provide a source of wealth as a mineral far more advantageous to Canada than merely as the domestic fuel it used to provide.
The demise of the domestic coal industry was brought about by the increasing availability and use of natural gas. My constituency has a very rich oil field and a heavy concentration of related oil fuel supply and service industries. We are blest therefore with a bountiful supply of cheap domestic and industrial fuel in the form of natural gas plus a large quantity of the natural resources required for the new and ever-growing petro-chemical and related industries. Not only do we have many large refineries but the people of my constituency are to a large extent employed in processing various chemical derivatives from coal tar. The processing of natural resources is carried on with other commodities as well such as in the nickel refining plant of the Sherritt Gordon Company Limited in the town of Fort Saskatchewan. All of these industries and wealth have served to emphasize and attach even more importance to the city of Edmonton as a supply and distribution centre. We are the most northern large city in Canada. Edmonton is a natural gateway and supply point to the Northwest Territories and the key communication centre for all travel to and from the Yukon territory, not only from western Canada but from the northwest part of the United States as well. There are those two major considerations that are of importance to Edmonton; one, the fact that it is located so far north that the weather is extremely important and, next, its location as the key communication centre to the northland.

The extremes of temperature are very wide and it can get cold in Edmonton in the winter, although if there is such a thing I believe I may say with pride that we have the most comfortable frigid climate in Canada. It is such a pleasant coldness I venture to say that one may freeze to death more comfortably in Edmonton than any place else. The carrying on of normal trade activities in the winter is possible but of course special techniques must be perfected and used if they are to be economically successful. The techniques often involve added cost and this is a factor which necessarily limits winter activities and contributes to our seasonal unemployment problem. I am happy to say that the businessmen of Edmonton have had many years of experience in overcoming weather difficulties as well as the transportation problems involved in supplying the north country. Edmonton has become the gateway to the north through the initiative, imagination and industry of its own businessmen who have continued to aid in the development of not only the west but the northwest. I am confident that government assistance will enable these same people to expand and develop the northland resources in the efficient and imaginative way that distinguishes private industry from cumbersome governmental undertakings.
I would be remiss if I did not bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that although Edmonton is a large commercial city, itself highly industrialized in a rich agricultural territory, and although it is the most northerly large city in Canada there are still tremendous distances to be covered to open up our northland resources. Edmonton itself is slightly south of the centre of Alberta and the northern part of that province is to a great extent wilderness relieved only by the small but very rich farm block of the Peace river country. The building of roads to develop resources would be of great benefit to all Canada. It is an undertaking so expensive that it is unfair to ask the relatively small population of Alberta to bear the cost unaided. This is one reason that dominion-provincial relations are of special interest to me and of vital importance to my constituents.
We would like to see better roads and more of them and we want the new railway to the north. We would like to have the Yellow-head route to the coast and we suggest it is only good business to select a route that is the shortest, utilizes the lowest passes, is less subject to blockage by snow and

would be a tremendous attraction to tourists. It would encourage Canadian as well as American tourists to travel to the west through Canada instead of through the United States. It would help to bring more traffic from the United States through the Canadian route instead of across the northern part of the United States and then up the west coast to the Alaska highway.
While I could talk for some time about my constituency I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I realize a member of parliament does not represent just one riding but must speak for all of Canada to the best of his ability and I would like to say just a few words on the broad aspects of the tasks before this house. I am most conscious of the fact that we who sit on the government side of the house somewhat outnumber the other parties in this house. I must say that my first impression judging from the amount of time spent on this debate and on other matters before the house by hon. members of the opposition parties is that they intend to make up by repetition what they lack in numbers. Perhaps I am being somewhat presumptuous in tendering advice to hon. members of the opposition in view of the fact that for the most part it is only seasoned veterans who have survived the activities of last year's campaigning but I am proceeding on the basis that they are not yet really seasoned veterans as members of the opposition, although I trust in the next several parliaments to come they will have the opportunity to remedy this slight defect.
We on this side of the house-and especially away out here in left field-know that we have a duty to give the government constructive criticism whenever we can. I should add that I know the wording of our criticism may not give hon. members of the opposition as much pleasure as the ringing denunciations they would likely use to phrase the same comments, but I believe a gentle reminder can be as fully effective in achieving remedies if any are necessary. I would perhaps not be going too far if I were to suggest that judging from some of the criticism heard in this house a gentle reminder might be much more effective simply because it would be such a great change.
I feel, sir, that hon. members have been most patient in listening to me, and I resume my seat only because of the honest fear that I might see this house reduced to a bare quorum if I continue. I hope that the goodwill earned in being brief is a good investment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate you on your election to your high office and to couple with
The Address-Mr. Knowles it congratulations to the Deputy Speaker. In so doing I do not wish to belabour the point, but simply and sincerely to echo the sentiments so ably expressed by previous speakers. Likewise, I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on a job well done.
I know that it must be gratifying to all hon. members to note that in the speech from the throne this government will take definite steps toward a northern development program so that our natural resources in this vast region may become available for the benefit of all Canadians. I hope that in the development of this new area we in this level of government as well as people in all levels of government will not lose sight of the need of a nationally planned use of our renewable resources, especially our top six inches of soil. In times of surplus and overproduction the importance of this great natural resource is often pushed into the background. However, we in Canada must constantly remind ourselves that this important national resource represents only about 11 per cent of our total area. It stretches in a perilously thin line across our country.
In my opinion the conservation of this vital natural resource is of paramount importance to all Canadians now living as well as to the countless millions yet unborn. Great empires of the past have risen and flourished only to fall with the loss of their top soil. Ancient cities of wealth and culture lie buried beneath drifting sands. Countless wars and famines bear witness to the potent role of soil in history. In fact, soil and soil erosion are part and parcel of the story of mankind.
While our federal government does not have jurisdiction over provinces and municipalities in respect of land use, yet it can help to promote conditions which are conducive to proper land use. It is important at this time in our development that we pause and give consideration to the mistakes of past civilizations as well as heed the frugal and careful practices of some of the older European civilizations which have survived through the centuries because they have learned to conserve those resources.
From these considerations we in Canada should develop a co-ordinated planned conservation program. The county of Norfolk which I represent, located on the north shore of lake Erie in southern Ontario, has over the past 30 years provided a good example of proper land use. While we do have modest factories and one of the largest fresh-water fishing fleets in Canada, yet agriculture is the basic source of our wealth.
Norfolk has long been famous for its fruits, particularly apples, peaches and berries. The

The Address-Mr. Knowles
eastern part of the county contains some of the finest dairy herds to be found anywhere. The western portion contains a light, sandy soil, easily given to wind erosion. In fact, as late as 40 years ago, this whole area through an improper type of farming presented a picture of deserted farms and drifting sand. Attempts were made in some instances to reforest certain areas in order to control the wind erosion. Today this whole trend is reversed, and the western sandy portion of the county now contributes its share of wealth to the county. The key to this remarkable economic recovery lies in the proper land use and good soil conservation practices related to the introduction and the growing of tobacco as a major farm crop. Never before was the marriage of soil and seed so profitable as that of the tobacco seed to the sandy soils of Norfolk county and surrounding areas.
I now propose to deal in some detail with the problems and economics relating to the production of tobacco. In as much as I am a tobacco grower myself, it is from firsthand knowledge that I discuss these matters. I think it would be of interest to hon. members to know that 99 per cent of the tobacco used in Canada is grown in this country. Since 1920, we have gone from a position where only 30 per cent of leaf tobacco was Canadian-grown, to the position where today 99 per cent of the tobacco smoked in Canada is grown in Canada. Of this total, approximately 50 per cent is grown in the county of Norfolk.
The production of flue-cured tobacco is a highly specialized one. Tobacco is generally the only crop grown on a farm and it requires a great deal of skill and knowledge of production practices on the part of the grower to ensure the quality of leaf desirable for manufacturing purposes. A large capital investment is required for the land, buildings and equipment and very large expenditures are required for labour, fertilizer and other ordinary operating expenses.
There is a high degree of risk in the production of tobacco since it is a crop which is very sensitive to changes in weather and is easily damaged by frost, wind and hail. The following is a list of losses over the past three years: in 1954, over 8 million pounds of tobacco were destroyed, which resulted in a loss of over $3,440,000; in 1955, one of the highest losses was sustained, amounting to 25 million pounds, to the value of $11 million; in 1956, 2 million pounds were destroyed, resulting in a loss of $920,000. I would just like to say that these losses are not losses that are spread over the total area. Generally, they strike in well-defined areas, causing losses to a few of the growers.
fMr. Knowles.]
Crop rotation, on a two-year basis, is practised, the alternative crop being rye, which is disked under and allowed to sprout the second year and is then plowed under. During the growing season much time and labour is spent on planting, spraying, hoeing and suckering. Harvesting generally commences in the early part of August and requires a great deal of labour. In fact, it is estimated that it requires an additional
40,000	labourers in the harvest season.
Once the leaf is harvested it is taken to a curing kiln where it is strung on to laths and then hung in the kilns where the curing operations take from four days to a week, depending on the kind of tobacco and the outside weather conditions. Curing again is a highly specialized job and can make or break a crop. The leaf is then removed to a pack barn where it remains until it is prepared for sale. After being purchased by the companies the tobacco is processed to bring it to a condition where it is packed in hogsheads and then allowed to age from 18 months to two years.
In the years that the tobacco growers have been organized, production has been controlled by the granting to each farm by the marketing board of a certain number of acres which could be planted to tobacco. These are known as marketing board rights and these rights could be sold or, at least, are sold, with the farm and the greater the growing rights the greater the value of the farm.
The cost per acre of growing tobacco is extremely high. The average farm contains about 100 acres of which approximately 80 acres are available for tobacco production. Based on a two-year rotation 40 acres are in crop each year. The average farm of 100 acres together with its buildings is valued at between $70,000 and $100,000. Taking 1,360 pounds per acre as the average yield and a price of 49 cents a pound, which was the average for 1957, each acre can produce something over $600. However, any bank manager in the tobacco belt will have figures to show that the cost of producing an acre of tobacco is anywhere from $500 to $600 leaving less than $100 per acre to cover depreciation, return on investment, management and risk. Thus it is apparent that while considerable capital is required the net profit is not so high in proportion as many are led to believe.
A few moments ago I referred to the fact that Canada produces 99 per cent of her tobacco leaf requirements, but in addition the tobacco growers have always produced over and above the needs of the home market. This additional production has found its way into the export trade, thereby making Canada

a tobacco exporting country. The United Kingdom has been our chief customer for this commodity. However, in this market as in other overseas markets our chief competitor has been the United States of America and we have also had competition from Rhodesia, both of which produce tobacco similar to our own leaf but in many cases of inferior quality grade for grade.
In the competition for overseas markets it has been argued that growers by their continuing struggle for a fair return on their investment were in danger of pricing themselves out of these markets. In this respect it should be pointed out that in the United States, a major exporting country, the price received for tobacco by growers was five cents above that received by Canadian producers averaged over the past seven years.
Again, in the matter of export it is interesting to note a quality comparison between Canadian and Rhodesian tobacco. Of the entire 1957 crop the two top grades represented	81	per	cent of	our Canadianproduction but represented only 60 per cent of the tobacco grown in Rhodesia, while the two lower grades were only 18 per cent of the Canadian production but were 39 per cent of the Rhodesian. These figures demonstrate that the quality of our product is superior	to	that	of	our	commonwealth
competitor.
Tobacco growers have always agreed with the proposition that Canada should produce sufficient	tobacco	for	export and havedemonstrated	this,	as	just	illustrated, by
keeping price demands within reason and quality above par. The quantity of tobacco produced has been regulated by acreage control, already mentioned, and growers have kept a careful watch on tobacco stocks lest by overproduction they might break down the price structure. They are always ready to produce all the tobacco needed to keep stocks on hand at a reasonable level and sufficient to supply the export requirements. However, no farmer growing a crop costing over $550 per acre to produce can afford to take the risk of having unsold tobacco left on his hands or the results of having to sell tobacco below the cost of production. Until he has a definite assurance that every pound he can produce can be sold at a reasonable price he will be definitely unwilling to produce to full capacity.
Perhaps the chief reason for this wariness in the matter of full production lies in the experiences of the past. In 1954, for example, farmers were urged by those who should know to grow full acreage resulting in a total production of 167,988,000 pounds which sold for 43.2 cents a pound and that year Canada exported only 30,087,370 pounds.
The Address-Mr. Knowles The following year, with large stocks on hand amounting to over 126 million pounds, the negotiated price was 45.4 cents for a crop totalling 112,202,000 pounds. That year we had an acreage cut of over 30 per cent while exports from the previous year's bumper crop rose to 45 million pounds. That has been the pattern generally. After a bumper crop exports have been considerably larger in the following year.
The number of pounds of tobacco which Canada may export in any given year is determined by two factors. The first is the amount the importer is willing and able to buy and the second is the amount our Canadian exporting companies are willing to release for export. Inasmuch as the grower has no direct control over these vital factors he is not ready to go into all-out production lest this exportable tobacco be called a surplus and used against him in negotiating a price in a given year.
In the April 18, 1958 issue of the United States magazine, Tobacco there appears the announcement that the United States government has increased its support price by 3.4 cents to 54.2 cents per pound for the 1958 crop which indicates a trend to increased prices for farm commodities to relieve the United States farmer from the cost-price squeeze. In Canada the tobacco grower to date has never asked the government to introduce a floor price whereby it might become necesary for the government to buy, process ^nd store tobacco. Through his own organization he has endeavoured to regulate his production, often under pressures, and so prevent the accumulation of depressing surpluses.
Last year the Ontario flue cured tobacco growers marketing board instituted a system of selling tobacco by the bale auction system using the Dutch clock and a negotiated minimum average price. On the whole the growers were well satisfied but in some instances the competitive bidding let the grade prices fall below the minimum average with the result that some individuals took unjustifiable losses.
After this situation developed a tobacco growers co-operative was formed and a small tobacco processing plant was purchased. A buyer for the co-operative then began bidding on the auction floor in an effort to bolster prices when need arose. However, due to lack of capital the co-operative's efforts were too small to produce the desired effect.
It is hoped by many tobacco growers in all parts of Ontario that the federal government legislation can be amended so that loans can be made available to the co-operative and to any other similar commodity co-operative endeavouring to maintain its price structure by its own efforts. It should be pointed out that tobacco processed and stored is one crop that

The Address-Mr. Knowles improves with age in proper storage so that the risk of loss in financing such a venture is practically nil. It is felt that a co-operative such as proposed will act as a cushion for both growers and buying companies to take up and hold any unforeseen surplus which may develop through ideal growing conditions. Such a surplus can easily be assimilated the following year through acreage reduction sufficient to meet the emergency.
It is deemed fair and just to seek federal assistance as outlined in view of the enormous revenue pouring into the federal treasury from the taxes levied against the tobacco industry as a whole. In the year 1956 a total of $285 million in excise taxes was collected by the tobacco industry for the federal treasury, which is actually four times the actual value of the tobacco crop itself.
-This reference to the revenue derived from tobacco brings me to the whole question of taxes levied on this highly specialized industry. On several occasions the tobacco marketing association of Ontario has waited upon former ministers of finance with carefully prepared briefs outlining its views on the taxes levied on the industry, which views were supported by accurate statistics, and requesting a reduction of taxation on tobacco products. It is hoped that our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will review this problem which is so vital to the producer of tobacco and accede to the request for relief in this connection. Past briefs have shown conclusively that a moderate tax reduction would increase the sales of cigarettes, thereby creating a greater demand for tobacco and the opportunity to expand our growing operations. A decrease in tobacco tax has also been proven to be advantageous to the government, because a reduced tax levy with resulting higher sales volume would yield more revenue than the present high rate of taxation with the existing sales volume. It should be noted that the accuracy of this prediction was proven when a small cut in tobacco taxation was granted back in 1952-53, resulting in higher sales and, within one year later, an increased revenue to the government of $7,800,000.
I have described in some detail this relatively new industry which is centred in the riding of Norfolk, because of its importance to Canada as a whole, as well as because of the fact the complexity of the growth and sale of this product are not widely known. I trust I have communicated to the house something of our accomplishments in the past and our hopes for the future in so far as the growing and marketing of tobacco is concerned.
Another problem which affects my riding of Norfolk is the plight of several of our

textile factories. This difficulty, however, is common to every textile producing centre across Canada. It is a situation about which many hon. members in this house are well informed. We now await the report of the tariff board. In conclusion, I should like to say that I hope proper action will soon be taken to remedy this serious problem.
Mr, Egan Chambers (St, Lawrence-St.
George): Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by adding my congratulations to those of others on your election to your very important office in this house. During the last parliament your reputation for fairness and urbanity spread well beyond the house itself. I am sure that people all over the country will join those who have spoken here in a feeling of satisfaction that you have again been chosen Speaker of this house.
(Translation):
At the same time, I wish to congratulate the chairman of the committee of the whole (Mr. Sevigny). In view of his reputation, we can be sure that he will discharge his duties with distinction.
(Text):
I believe it is customary to take advantage of this debate, particularly during a maiden speech, to say something about the constituency which has honoured you by choosing you as its member of parliament. I should like to do that. Before I do so, perhaps it would be in order to tell the house some of the biases that will form the background for what I will say from time to time here. Perhaps I should say, putting it another way, something about my political beliefs. In the first place, I consider myself a liberal, in the sense that term was understood in the last century and is understood in most countries of the world today. Perhaps I could illustrate what I mean by quoting from an article by Mr. Marcus Long in the April issue of the Canadian Commentator.
I quote:
The philosophy of liberalism is the best philosophy for Canada. The Conservative party, through Mr. Diefenbaker, has embraced it. The C.C.F. party in its Winnipeg manifesto embraced it. If we can only persuade the Liberal party to embrace it, the future is full of promise.
I might say that what I have heard from the C.C.F. so far in this parliament seems closer to Regina than to Winnipeg. What I understand by this philosophy is that it concerns itself with the individual before the group or the class, not that the group and class do not need to be considered. But when we ignore the individual citizen or place his interests below what we conceive to be the interests of some group, as the socialists do, we start to recede from the level of democracy and civilization that we have reached

and move back towards feudalism. The so-called classless society is in fact the epitome of the classified society.
A government of Canada which concerns itself with the rights of individuals is not only an admirable but a necessary thing. This is a country of great opportunity. We have, as has so often been said, tremendous natural resources to be developed. We have a great task before us in expanding our processing industries, thus providing more employment for our people. This kind of development has always been best accomplished in a climate of opportunity. The role of government in such a society is one of encouragement, and regulation to prevent exploitation. The government is also the medium through which we undertake those major projects that are the concern of the whole country and that are beyond the capacity of the individual. It is through the government also that we discharge those responsibilities that we all have, to ensure that no citizen shall suffer through circumstances that are not of his own making. The line between what is the government's responsibility and what should be left to the individual citizen is sometimes hard to define. Perhaps it will be easier if we always start from the position that every Canadian is free to do whatever he wishes, except certain things that are withheld for the good of the community as a whole, rather than starting, as the socialists do, by saying that no one is allowed to do anything except what the government permits him to do.

The constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George is at the very heart of the city of Montreal, the metropolis of Canada. Its people include the various racial groups making up the Canadian nation: 35 per cent of it is French-speaking and there are people of Ukrainian, Polish, Russian, Greek, German, Italian, Scottish, Irish, English origins and several others. All events throughout Canada affect this constituency. If agriculture in western Canada is affected, our workers in the transportation business and our grain brokers are affected. If the government builds a highway in northern Canada, it will find part of the required machinery and equipment in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George. It can be said with the former secretary of war in the United States... "What is good for Canada is good for St. Lawrence-St. George, and what is good for St. Lawrence-St. George is good for Canada."
That is why it is a great pleasure for me to support the proposals made in the speech
The Address-Mr. Chambers from the throne we heard last week. This speech suggests a legislative program dealing with all problems besetting Canada at the present time and I hope our friends of other parties will not prevent the carrying out of this program.
I am not one of those who say that the St. Lawrence seaway will be a source of new income for the city of Montreal. It will serve the welfare of the whole of Canada and we of Montreal will have to sacrifice something for our country, but the seaway will reduce business in our area. For instance, grain which is usually delivered in Montreal by trains and ship, to be trans-shipped overseas will in the future be carried in seagoing ships that will be loaded in the very ports of lake Superior. In the future, freight trains arriving in Montreal with their load destined to Ontario and western Canada will by-pass Montreal. In my opinion there is only one solution to this problem. It will be to maintain navigation throughout the winter on the St. Lawrence river.
I therefore hope the government will take this suggestion under serious consideration. (Text):
I realize that the opening of the St. Lawrence river during the winter is a project of large proportions. But so is the St. Lawrence seaway. I realize that the cost of such a project might be considerable. But the cost of the seaway is considerable. I believe that the advantages to be gained for the country in general and the district of Montreal in particular will amply justify the expense involved. Some hon. members might say that this project is beyond our capabilities. But in an age where we are able to put satellites into orbit around the earth and where science has developed engines of destruction that stagger the imagination we need not feel that the controlling of our environment for the benefit of our people to the extent of melting some ice is beyond our abilities. I therefore hope that the government will undertake a thorough and serious investigation of this project.
I was glad to note that the speech from the throne included an undertaking for the vigorous promotion of international trade. The steps that were taken by the government during the last parliament were, in my view, admirable and have already given signs of bearing excellent fruit. However, there are other areas wherein our trade can be improved and one that has been mentioned is the United States. The speeches which have been made by some of the ministers in the United States and in Canada and which have received prominent mention in the United States press have been, in my view, along the right lines.

The Address-Mr. Chambers In some cases they were criticized. But what the Americans understand best of all is publicity. We shall get nowhere in improving our trade position in the United States by hiding our light under a bushel. I therefore hope that that type of activity, particularly in approaches informal if necessary, to congress and to congressmen on behalf of an expansion of Canadian trade and more favourable import duties under the United States laws will be continued during the life of this parliament.
There has been some talk this afternoon about the political position in the province of Quebec. It seems that very few people can think of the province of Quebec without thinking of politics. However, I think that one of the most encouraging results that emerged from the last election for the future of this country was the result obtained by the Conservative party in the province of Quebec. I would say this, though perhaps some hon. members who just applauded will not agree with me: I hope the day never comes when the Conservative party holds in the province of Quebec the type of majority that the Liberal party has held in the past. I hope that in that province we shall continue having a vote based on the national issues, having our citizens vote for the same reason that citizens vote in every other part of the country. I hope that the members of this house from the province of Quebec will in the future be able to represent-as I think they do in this house-all the political points of view that exist in that province.
I should like at this time, to express my thanks to the electors of St. Lawrence-St. George who on March 31 did me the great honour of choosing me as their member in this house. I do not know whether I would be out of order at this time in also thanking that somewhat smaller group of electors in St. Lawrence-St. George who tried to do the same thing last June, or the even smaller group who tried to send me here from St. Antoine-Westmount in 1954, or the quite small group that tried to send me here from St. Antoine-Westmount in 1953. But I should like to say that I am equally as grateful to those who tried as I am to those who so recently were successful. I will try in this house to justify the confidence that was placed in me by those voters on those four different occasions.
There is one thing, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to comment on with regard to what I have read in Hansard in the past and what I have heard since I have been here. I have noticed that hon. members will sometimes resurrect an old copy of Hansard and will say to the previous speaker that in 1941 he said so and so and that he has just risen
[Mr. Chambers.!
and said the opposite. May I say that times change and circumstances alter. But aside from that, as I sit here and listen to other hon. members addressing this house, I hope that I shall grow in wisdom so that in future years I may not feel the same way on some policies as I do today. I give warning that if in the future I am quoted against myself I will not be afraid to say simply that I have changed my mind.
I do not wish to resume my seat on this occasion without saying something about my feelings for the House of Commons. I have been among the strangers in this place on many occasions. I sat here on two memorable Fridays during the pipe line debate and watched and listened while a little group of members fought one of the most memorable fights in the history of any parliament to preserve for the people of this country the right to be heard in a free parliament through their elected representatives. I have read the history of parliaments and the other fights that have been waged to keep tyranny at bay. I hope, sir, and I pray that when I leave this place for whatever reason, it may never be said of me that I did anything to lessen the dignity or the prestige of the House of Commons, which is the keeper of all our ancient rights and privileges.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafre-niere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They both acquitted themselves with distinction and their respective constituents can be assured that they will be well represented in this parliament.
I would like to congratulate you, sir, on your appointment, and from my brief stay in the house and seeing you perform your duties, it is easy to understand the great confidence which the members on both sides of the house have in you.
I must say that 1 am very happy to be here as a supporter of the Conservative government, and I have great faith in our Prime Minister and the hon. members of his cabinet. I am sure that this government will give the people of this great nation the best legislation possible.
The constituency of Selkirk, which I have the privilege of representing, is the most historic constituency in the province of Manitoba. I believe it was the first constituency in the province of Manitoba and the first man to be elected to represent it was Donald A. Smith, who later became Lord Strathcona. He was a member of Sir John A. Macdonald's government. The last time this constituency was represented by a Conservative was from 1930 to 1935, when Mr. James H. Stitt was the member. He is now a resident of Ottawa.
In area the constituency is very large. Within its boundaries we have two great lakes, lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba. All the land between these lakes, starting with the town of Selkirk and the town of Stonewall to the south, reaches to Norway House to the north. This area is commonly known as the interlake area.
In the Selkirk constituency we have some of the best soil in Canada. The area around Stonewall is one of the highest producing pieces of land in the country. We also have marginal lands and some poor land; also large areas of pasture land, hay land and large herds of cattle. This constituency is different from any other in Canada because of the great variation in the soil and the two 57071-3-19
The Address-Mr. Stefanson great lakes within its boundaries. This constituency will have problems peculiar to it alone which will have to be dealt with on their individual merits.
The people of the Selkirk constituency come from many racial origins. I believe there are something like 24 racial origins represented and each one of these groups has contributed to the culture of this country and today, as never before, we are all truly Canadians and citizens of this country on an equal basis. I could go on at length outlining the contribution of the various groups, but I am sure it has often been expounded in the house before. These people work in industry, in offices and in business. Others are professional people. Some have businesses of their own. By far the largest group are our primary producers who consist of farmers, fishermen, trappers, mink ranchers, loggers, and so on. The farmers are by far the largest group and they produce wheat, barley, oats, flax, rye and various types of grass seeds, cattle, hogs, lambs, poultry, butter, milk, cream, eggs and vegetables. With all this production in agriculture we are fortunate to have a good Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) to find markets for all of these commodities.
The agricultural stabilization bill was welcomed generally by farmers. The vote on March 31 in western Canada indicated that. However, farmers are badly in need of farm credits and I am glad to see this item in the throne speech; likewise, crop insurance and soil conservation.
Several hon. members have mentioned fishing on the east and west coasts. I would like to say here that the fresh-water fishing in Manitoba is a major industry and produces some of the best fish in Canada. Like agriculture, this industry needs to be stabilized. Greater help could be rendered through research, conservation and sales promotion. Lake Manitoba has just a winter fishing season, while lake Winnipeg has three fishing seasons, namely winter fishing and two seasons on open water in the fall and summer. March 31 last was the first time for many years that those fishermen were not disfranchised. They are generally away north on the lake when elections are held and are unable to vote. There should be some means of setting up advance polls for fishermen. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean), being a maritimer, is well acquainted with coastal fishing and no doubt coastal fishing is a large industry. I would like to extend an invitation to the minister to visit the fishing grounds on lake Winnipeg at his convenience.

The Address-Mr. Stefanson I wish to congratulate this government on the legislation which they introduced in the twenty-third parliament. I will not go into detail on this legislation as the vote on March 31 clearly indicated how the people received it.
The proposed legislation in the speech from the throne indicates that the government will continue to bring in legislation for the benefit of all the people of Canada. The bill on unemployment insurance and the bill on national housing are clear indications of this. The bill on national housing can be of help to those building houses in small towns such as are found in my constituency. A vigorous program of public works will be appreciated by all. This also can be of benefit to my constituency. The proposed legislation having to do with small businesses will be appreciated also by many of my constituents.
This government has indicated its willingness to meet municipal officials to discuss their problems. This is most welcome, as I think all municipalities today are experiencing difficulty meeting demands made on them because of their limited income from real estate taxes. Originally the real estate tax was never intended to assist in the financing of education and health and welfare. Somewhere along the line this obligation was handed to municipal officials who did not object at the time, but who are now trying to hand it back to the provincial governments, without success. Any town experiencing difficulty in making improvements in water and sewer installations and which has the initiative to do these things should be able to get help from a higher form of government.
One of the complaints which I have received on numerous occasions in my constituency has been with regard to the unsatisfactory television reception, especially since the change of the Winnipeg station from channel four to channel three. A large area of my constituency also is not serviced with television. Anything which the government can do to correct or assist in these matters will be appreciated. I have several other problems which will be referred to the ministers concerned.
At this time I should like to say that ^ I represent the most versatile constituency in Canada. The visitor will appreciate the many small towns spread throughout the countryside and in his travels he will admire the grain fields, the dairy herds, the hay meadows, the pasture land and the large herds grazing on those meadows. He also will find some of the most beautiful beaches in Canada on the west shore of lake Winnipeg and on the east shore of lake Manitoba.


Many hon. members have visited different parts of my constituency and I am sure they will always be made welcome no matter where or what part they visit. On the first Monday of August of each year we hold the annual Icelandic celebration in the beautiful park at Gimli. As president of the committee I extend an invitation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to hon. members of the house to be with us on that occasion to enjoy a day of relaxation among the evergreens on the shore of lake Winnipeg, where the Icelanders first landed and settled in 1875.
In concluding, sir, I would like to say that anybody sitting as a member of parliament should not be petty or small but should be here to work for the best interests of Canada as a whole. However, as the elected member for Selkirk, I will endeavour to represent all the people of the constituency fairly and with the best of my ability.
Financial demands on all levels of government, whether they be municipal, provincial or federal, are always getting greater and greater. As members of this house it is our duty to see that only just demands are answered. As individuals we should recognize and cherish the rights and privileges we now enjoy and if each and every one of us believes in giving an honest day's work for an honest day's pay and if we can convince enough people to do likewise the economy of this country will always be sound.
I would also like to suggest that this government is not only strong numerically, it also has great ability.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to your attention and the attention of this

The Address-Mr. Smallwood house the importance of agriculture to the Canadian economy. I shall read from the speech from the throne:
Unremitting efforts are being made to sell Canadian agricultural and fisheries products in the markets of the world and considerably larger exports of wheat and cattle have been made. Support prices have now been established for a considerable number of products under the Agricultural Stabilization Act to carry into effect, for the current year, the desire of parliament that agriculture should be thus assisted to realize fair returns for its labour and investment.
I am interested in the last part which reads:
-the desire of parliament that agriculture should be thus assisted to realize fair returns for its labour and investment.
This situation in which western farmers find themselves goes back to 1953 when the price of wheat dropped and the price of machinery and other commodities increased. In 1946 I bought a power binder for $460; ten years later that same binder cost $1,060. In 1953 a combine cost $5,600, and three years later the same piece of machinery sold for $6,400. This is just one example of the cost-price squeeze in which the farmers of Canada are caught. I am very happy to note that this government is trying to introduce legislation to ensure that the farmers of Canada receive their fair share of the national income. We cannot continue to operate with wheat at the price it is today, compared to the price we must pay for machinery.
What is the result of this situation? The farmers stop buying and there is unemployment in the factories, a general slowdown right across the country. In my locality this spring the reverse of this situation was quite noticeable. The price of cattle increased to the extent that it put money in the hands of farmers. The local machine agents sold more machinery this spring than they had for some years past. This had an effect on the prosperity of our community and on the unemployment situation right across Canada. I feel that western Canada is the greatest market for eastern factory products, so long as we are receiving sufficient money for our products. Agriculture is the backbone of our great country.
We have been subsidizing industry for the last few years. During the war we sold wheat to Great Britain at a price which was far below the world level. I am very proud that we contributed to the war effort to that extent, but I do not see why the farmers of western Canada had to carry the cost of that subsidy when it should have been carried by the national treasury. I suggest to our government that we work out a two-price 

system for wheat in order that we may receive our fair share of the national income.
May I again quote from the speech from the throne?
The act to provide cash advances on farm-stored grain has proven to be of advantage to a large number of farmers and to the economy as a whole. Certain amendments will be proposed to that act in the light of experience in its application.
This act, which provides cash advances on farm-stored grain, was a great boon to the economy of Canada last fall. It put money into the hands of the farmers when they needed it. I recall the former minister of agriculture getting up in the House of Commons and telling the members that this act was useless; that it could not possibly work; that the farmers did not want it and that the Liberals had a better system of bank loans. I ask you, what happened? In the first three months the farmers drew over twice as much money from this scheme as they borrowed from the banks under the Liberal program in three years. One can see, therefore, that the farmers like this act, and I do not notice that little fellow from Saskatchewan sitting in the opposition today.
Again I read from the speech from the throne:
Amendments will also be proposed to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act-
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was introduced under a Liberal government and was always unjust to the farmers and this year was no exception. Under this act now, many farmers who deserve payment are left out completely. I was very pleased to read in the throne speech that this act would be amended. I might say that I have a few amendments to it to present to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness).
There is a situation existing right across Canada under which it is nearly impossible for a young man to buy a farm. The result is that these young, prospective farmers are going to the cities to look for work, thus aggravating the unemployment situation. I propose to our government, as a remedy, that we immediately introduce a measure under which these young farmers may obtain a long-term loan at a reasonable rate of interest for the purchase of farms.
I hope the government will give serious consideration to the commencement of a second trans-Canada highway via the Yellow-head route through northern Alberta. This highway is long overdue and would be one more works program to relieve unemployment.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I have come to the House of Commons to give the people of Battle River-Camrose good representation and I shall do

my best to carry out that undertaking. Canada has a great future, and as a member of this government I shall work with my colleagues to unite this country from coast to coast so that our people may live in security.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy at the outset to congratulate you on your renewed appointment to the important post of Speaker of this house. During the 23rd parliament, when you were entrusted with the same duties, we who sat here at the time were able to appreciate your competence exercised with a remarkable sense of impartiality, your gentlemanliness, your sense of humour, your fine understanding. I am happy that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) supported by my leader, has once more nominated you to that post. I offer you my most sincere good wishes in this heavy task and in the discharge of the great responsibilities which are yours.
While this is no reflection on yourself personally, I would nevertheless like to remind the house that I hope that the tradition which consists of alternating French-speaking and English-speaking speakers will not be done away with. Of course I understand that since the 23rd parliament lasted only a few months, it was normal, under circumstances such as those, that you be reappointed to the post whose responsibilities you had discharged with such alertness, but I insist once more on the fact that this tradition of which I have just spoken should be re-established in the next parliament. We are reassured on that score by the appointment of a Frenchspeaking Canadian as deputy speaker, in the person of the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) to whom I offer also my most sincere congratulations.
During the last campaign I was privileged to be present at a political forum organized by the chamber of commerce of Montreal, at which the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) faced the hon. member for Longueuil. The hon. member for Laurier had stated at the time that the member for Longueuil was a man to be feared, as much because of his height as because of his knowledge. Before the last elections in 1957, there had been talk of nominating the now member for Longueuil as Conservative candidate in the constituency of Dollard. I must admit that I prefer to see the hon. member sitting for Longueuil rather than for Dollard and I was quite happy when he decided to run
The Address-Mr. Rouleau in Longueuil instead. I wish him every success as Deputy Speaker as well as a happy political career.
I would also like to offer my most heartfelt congratulations to the two new Quebec ministers: the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) and the new Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche). I was well acquainted with the new Secretary of State when we were both law students at the University of Montreal, some years ago. At that time, even if we were good friends, we did not see eye to eye on political problems, my good friend being a deep dyed nationalist, whereas I was a Canadian pure and simple. He has become a convert to Toryism whereas I remained convinced that Liberalism is still the political philosophy best suited to ensure the greatness of our country and the well being of our people. I am convinced that, even though we do not sit on the same side of the house, we shall remain excellent friends; I have no doubt that the new minister will devote all his talents to the service of his country.
Finally, I wish to congratulate the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Lafreniere and Mr. Nielsen). I am glad that the Prime Minister has seen fit to invite two young Canadians to play this traditional role in our parliamentary institutions.
It is gratifying to see such a great number of young Canadians in this house. It is a sign of the vitality of our parliamentary institutions and a guarantee for the future of our young and prosperous country.
Allow me also, Mr. Speaker, to express my heartfelt congratulations to the Prime Minister for his brilliant victory on March 31st last. It was not only a victory for the Conservative party but also a personal victory for the Prime Minister. He is an indefatigable worker, a convincing speaker, a man whose strong personality has impressed the whole country. His victory has been brilliant, even crushing.
The present Prime Minister, when he sat on the opposition side, always took pride in upholding the rights of parliament, of parliamentary institutions, of democracy and of the minorities. With the overwhelming majority he now has, there is perhaps a danger that he may forget the stand he took while sitting in the opposition, but I trust that he will remember the words that his revered mother said to him on the night of his victory. In fact, it is with emotion that we read in the newspapers the day after the election the

The Address-Mr. Rouleau words reported by the Prime Minister as coming from his mother who urged him to accept his victory with humility and to govern with discretion. Knowing the Prime Minister,
I am aware of the respect he must have for his mother and for her advice. I have no doubt that he will make it a point to follow such sound advice. As I live myself with my mother, whom I revere, I know to what extent a mother's advice can be precious to a man, especially to a politician. Once again, I am quite sure that when the Prime Minister will be inclined to forget himself, he will remember his mother's words and not encroach upon the rights and prerogatives to which minorities and more especially the opposition are entitled. The present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) my chief, has clearly established in the course of this debate the position which the Liberal party intends to take during this parliament. He was clear in his statement and he also reminded the Prime Minister of certain words he had said while he was in the opposition.
I congratulate the Leader of the Opposition for his splendid statement and I also congratulate him for the vigorous electoral campaign he has carried across the country. He proposed to the people an election platform capable of checking the unemployment crisis under which we are unfortunately labouring at the present time. I do not think the people have rejected the leader of the Liberal party nor the program he was advocating.

I can read it over, if you wish. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance,-excuse me, I am going to speak slowly because this may be of some use to you. The Minister of Finance, in preparing his present budget should seriously consider the briefs submitted to the Prime Minister by the Chamber of Commerce of Montreal requesting an amendment to the federal income tax act. The Minister of Finance should take into careful consideration the two important findings of the brief I just mentioned, that is (1) income tax should not ordinarily be levied against the income necessary to the subsistence of the taxpayer and his family; (2) above that necessary minimum, income tax should equalize the sacrifice between taxpayers.
With our present high cost of living, I believe that the basic tax exemption should be $3,000 for married people, with an additional exemption of $600 per child, and $1,500 for
The Address-Mr. Rouleau single persons. With less than this minimum amount, it is entirely impossible for a family and for any individual to live decently and acquire the bare necessities of life.
I also want to suggest another amendment to the federal income tax act. Since the war, there have been certain changes in the Canadian way of life, particularly in the large centres, while city dwellers are progressively leaving the downtown areas for the suburbs. As a direct consequence of this condition, industrial and other workers, as well as members of the professions in a general way, have to travel great distances to work. Though quite a few use the public transportation system, a greater number still are forced to travel by car from their home to their place of occupation.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the expenses incurred, both with regard to public transportation as well as automobile travel, could be deducted from the income tax. It seems to me that this would be a fair and just measure for workers as well as for business men, industrialists and professional men.
I have another suggestion to offer to the Minister of Finance. For some years now there has been talk of the growing needs of education. In this house I have more than once requested that we should provide assistance for our students within constitutional limits in the federal area. I return to this matter today and I would ask the Minister of Finance to do something for education without infringing on provincial autonomy. To help parents and students, we should find a way to grant more university scholarships, and also to allow those parents who have children in college or university, as well as those students who have to work to pay for their studies, to deduct the tuition fees from their income tax, whether it be for tuition fees themselves, or for books and instruments required for the various courses, as well as living expenses incurred by students who have to live in another city. In other words, all expenses incurred by the student.
By increasing the purchasing power of families as well as of individual citizens, these various income tax deductions which I have just listed would be of immediate help to Canadian families and would I am sure considerably reduce present unemployment.
A few moments ago I said that I was not opposed to the large public works which the

The Address-Mr. Rouleau present government has in mind. However,
I wish to state once more that I do not believe that this type of undertaking will materially reduce unemployment. In order to reduce unemployment, especially in large centres, it would be easy for the government to carry out certain projects in the larger cities of this country. The federal government might, within the limits of its jurisdiction, contribute to the general programs of the larger cities and undertake some major projects. In a large city like Montreal, for instance, where the government could build a throughway in the harbour area along the St. Lawrence which is under the National Harbours Board, the heavy traffic of the Canadian metropolis might thus be diverted and jobs created for hundreds and hundreds of unemployed in Montreal.
This is only one instance of what the government could do to remedy the unemployment crisis we are experiencing to-day.
The government might, moreover, immediately proceed with a complete clearance of slums in large Canadian centres. At the instigation of the Liberal government, the city of Montreal has already undertaken the clearance of a slum area in the metropolis. In fact, a slum district of Montreal was cleared in which it is proposed to carry out what is commonly called the Dozois plan. This plan was much discussed in Montreal and I do not want to express an opinion even on the nature of the plan. One thing is certain however: thanks to the co-operation of various agencies, thanks specially to the generous support of the federal government, we are witnessing the clearance of hundreds of slums in Montreal which will be replaced by sanitary housing. This plan, which will cost 13 million dollars, half of it to be paid by the federal government, will provide approximately 3,000 jobs for a period of three years.
According to experts of the city of Montreal, there are at the present time 52 areas which can be improved, 12 of which are favourable to the carrying out of a plan such as the one I just mentioned. In order to do something useful while at the same time providing jobs for the unemployed, it is urgent that the government proceed without delay with the clearance of the slums of those 12 areas which include 10,000 substandard houses. Those slums could be replaced by houses which could be made available to wage-earners at prices within their reach and by

houses which could be rented jointly by the city of Montreal and the federal government at family rents, that is to say, rents which, instead of being set arbitrarily, could be set at a rate equivalent to a week's salary of the tenant, with an adequate reduction for each dependent child.
I firmly believe that in heeding those suggestions, the government would do service to the low wage-earner and at the same time would relieve unemployment. I believe that this would also be an indirect way of helping municipalities without having to wait for the federal-provincial-municipal conference which the Prime Minister promised before June 10.
It is the present Solicitor General, my excellent friend the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who pointed out to the house in the session of November 1953, and I quote from the official record of the debates of the session of 1953-54, Vol. 1, page 67:
The lamentable financial state of the municipalities is therefore evidence that a new conference is essential so that our federal financial system may be reviewed, and with an open mind, in order that each administrative body, either federal, provincial or municipal should be in a position to be master of its own destinies and in order that everyone be treated with justice and equity.
Since those words were spoken, I believe that nothing has been done to alleviate the burden of municipalities and that, as far as federal-provincial relations are concerned, no new or concrete proposals came out of the federal-provincial conference. Now I wish to quote again the Solicitor General of Canada, because I feel that what he was saying at the time is right to the point when we read the speech from the throne of this year:
. . . Unfortunately, the speech from the throne says nothing about a federal-provincial conference, and we all know that the people of Quebec would like such a conference to be called, in order to allow the governments concerned to reach some kind of agreement. Each particular government must be able to collect the moneys which it needs for the conduct of its affairs, and I deem it to be antidemocratic when in a federal state one of the component parts is forced to come and beg regularly from the other part the necessary funds.
I think that the federal government departs from the principles of the constitution when it lays its hands on all sources of taxation, exhausts them and then meddles in fields of activity that are not its concern, even if it offers sums of money. There is a way to settle the matter once and for all. The provinces should have the authority to levy themselves the money they need: they would, in turn, give the municipalities their autonomy and, in this way, a certain balance would be possible. I am sure it would benefit our Canadian democracy.
Those words of the Solicitor General adequately sum up the policy supposedly

advocated by the premier of the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne I offer my most sincere congratulations and to you, Mr. Speaker, and to your deputy I also extend good wishes. To the people of my riding I extend sincere thanks for their support. Although there were approximately 1,200 Liberal supporters in my riding on election day there are very few since then. Despite the fact that there may be those in my riding who are against us they know that we shall never be against them.
The appeal that we made in the last election was to invite all men of good will regardless of past political affiliation to join us, not only to support us on election day but to give us a hand in the days that lie ahead to procure for this country the best government Canada ever had and also the best government this world has ever known. That is our aim and avowed purpose. I take pleasure in extending the invitation to all hon. members opposite to do the same.
Of course, as the dust settles over the ruin and destruction, and in one instance the complete disappearance, of the opposing political parties it may be well for us to pause to note that our victory was achieved in no small way by the default of the other parties and especially the Liberal party whose lack of a program was summed up in one irrelevant and desperate promise to cut the taxes of Canada's 600,000 unemployed, whose spotty and scanty unemployment insurance benefits hardly put them in a bracket to pay income tax. In patting ourselves on the back let us not do so too enthusiastically and let us not forget that if many people voted for us they had little else to vote for as an alternative. Possibly we did not offer all the measures that are needed but certainly we offered more.

The Address-Mr. Van Horne
I hasten to speak, not without sorrow, of a most urgent problem affecting most severely over 8,000 men in my riding and more than
600,000	people in Canada. There is more unemployment and more suffering due to unemployment in my riding today than at any time since the darkest days of the depression.
I regard it as my duty to tell this house that if it were not for unemployment insurance, family allowances and pensions many people in my constituency-

-would be close to insurrection. It is all very well for us to put the blame for this recession-and in my riding no other word describes it-where it so rightly belongs, on the former dead, lacklustre, unapproachable Liberal regime but it is a sacred duty of this government to take the immediate, fully effective, result-producing and even drastic measures now needed to put our people to work. In this respect we must recognize that this government has succeeded in doing more than any other government in the history of Canada.
However, I have in my riding actual privation and poverty due to unemployment. In many homes the cupboards are bare and children are hungry, cold and sick. This condition is not entirely new. This situation existed to almost the same extent under every government but I for one warned and warned again and again the former Liberal administration that their cruel, senseless and unnecessary policies in regard to tight money and foreign trade and their indifference to maritime rights and needs would bring about and were creating the very pitiful and unfortunate circumstances from which suffer well over 10,000 families in my riding.
But they would not listen and they stayed aloft on the high pedestal on which they had perched themselves, too self-important to listen, too self-hallowed to act, too lazy to wake up until the morning of June 11, 1957, when their sense of smugness in their own infallibility was cut from under them. It was then too late; it was all over for them. They were out as I told them they would be if they did not smarten up. Then they floundered about unable to be a worthwhile opposition or an effective one because almost every time they tried to criticize and oppose they found themselves automatically pointing at their own sins and deficiencies while in office and which we unfortunately are too slow in correcting, changing or altering.
We were great in the opposition at recognizing the faults of the old Liberal regime but we were and we are a bit too slow in correcting them now that we are in office.

After June 10 I told this government in letter after letter directed to the heads of it and in warning after warning that we would have more unemployment in my riding and in Canada during the winter of 1957 and 1958 than at any time since the depths of the depression unless immediate and even drastic measures were taken. I spelled out the measures I felt were vitally needed not only to provide work but to fulfil long-felt needs the unfulfilment of which had held back for so long the economic development of my riding and my region.
In this country we see a mysterious, a unique phenomenon; in this cherished land which we call Canada, where every man, every citizen, is potentially the richest man on earth, thousands of innocent children suffer from hunger, cold and want. For what partially effective measures this government has taken I am most grateful. This government has undertaken to do more for my riding in seven months than all other governments put together have done since confederation, and this applies generally to the entire Atlantic provinces.
But these projects-and I speak only of my riding now-are scarcely started although they were approved many months ago. Unfortunately, far too many members of the top echelon of the civil service did not catch the urgency to cut red tape and to move quickly. There was this Liberal "can't-be-done" defeatist attitude, which was one of the main causes why so many people are getting the impression that the well conceived and salutary program of public works has for several reasons bogged down. In times such as these, with so many men in need of work, urgency and red tape cutting are requisites. We simply cannot operate at the snail's pace for which the old regime was noted and for which it was kicked out of office. But this unfortunate condition does not detract from the hitherto unknown spirit of co-operation and dedication to duty which characterize every member of this government.
No man in the history of Canada has done more to point the way to a better Canada and to the fulfilment of the needs of all our people than the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). It is unfortunate that the more immediate means necessary to implement our program are not being taken now. Certainly, it is axiomatic to note how long we had to wait and how far west we had to go to get a Minister of Public Works who would launch, in co-operation with the supporters of the government, a whole new deal for the maritime provinces and for all of Canada.
But, I ask that the decks be cleared for action. I ask that we move more quickly and

more swiftly. If we need another 100 engineers to get these projects moving now, for goodness sake, let us get another 100 engineers. All honest means at our command must be taken now to put our people to work. The senior civil servants, or many of the civil service-and I detract nothing from their skill and their dedication and loyalty to Canada-must be made to get in step with the government's plan and policy. They must be made to keep in step. We must have action now when it is needed.
This, sir, leads me to the problem of unemployment insurance and labour policies generally. I am grateful to see that the period in which seasonal benefits may be drawn has been extended for those who have sufficient stamps. How many times must I tell you that this is not enough? What is urgently needed, is a complete overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act so that its provisions will correspond to the policies of our party, which will ensure justice and due consideration and the rights of unemployment insurance benefits to all those who need unemployment insurance benefits.
Let me tell you how the majority of the workers in my riding are affected and penalized by the present unemployment insurance regulations. Our people live on small holdings, small farms, and they follow the seasons. They work in the woods. A man will work for possibly six weeks in the spring on the drive. During that time he will get unemployment insurance stamps; he may get six stamps. He comes back home and he sows his crop; during that time he gets no stamps. Later on in the summer he may get a few weeks' casual work on the roads on construction, and so on. He may get stamps for that. He may work four weeks and he will have a total of 10 stamps. Then he has to go back and take in his crop and he gets no stamps. He may work for a while on the farm and for this he gets no stamps at all. He may go into the woods, follow the operation, for which he may get four, five or six stamps, so he ends up with perhaps 15 stamps; but many of our people have only 14 and they cannot qualify for unemployment insurance and they cannot get their benefits.
I repeat now, the urgent recommendations I made to this government on January 21 last, namely the complete abolition of all waiting periods. There is nothing more unjust than those waiting periods for unemployment insurance. A person should receive benefits for each stamp for as long as he is out of work, based on a scale which would guarantee at least $2 per week per stamp, up to the present minimum values, and then all 57071-3-201
The Address-Mr. Van Horne benefits should be increased to at least one-half of the worker's salary and for as long as a person is out of work because work is unavailable for him. There should be an abolition of all delays. There should be benefits in case of sickness where such sickness necessitates lay-offs. There should be unemployment benefits for those who, like farmhands, woodworkers and those doing certain kinds of farm work, who even though they are not on the payroll, are to all intents and purposes workmen in every sense of the word. They should be included in unemployment insurance benefits.
I note that an agreement has not yet been made whereby 6,000 men who work in the state of Maine could have their stamps recognized in Canada. I understand two letters were written. I demand more effective action and as long as these improvements are left undone our workers will continue to suffer merely for want of proper consideration and action. I ask this government to complete the necessary agreement with the state of Maine so that our 6,000 Canadians who work in Maine will be able to get unempolyment insurance when they return to their homes because they contributed in the state of Maine when they were there. This is a problem that I took up with the old government. I take it up again with this one. I tell you now, as I have said before, many families in my riding suffer at this very moment severe and crippling hardships because the things I have just mentioned have not been done.
Let me pass quickly to the Canadian National Railways. When our hard-pressed potato farmers found prices running last spring at $4 a barrel they asked for reefer cars in St. Leonard, 25 miles from Edmund-ston, so they could ship their potatoes and get the higher price for their potatoes. They were told there were no reefer cars available but on the very day they were told this some 70 reefer cars were lying idle in the C.N.R. yards in Edmundston. Those reefer cars were made available to us two weeks later when the price of potatoes had fallen to $2 a barrel because of the United States dumping of potatoes on the Canadian market.
Lay-offs in my riding seem calculated to create the greatest hardship for men whose long years of service and the faithful performance of their duties certainly entitled them to better and more just consideration. Some men were laid off for good who had only two or three months more to go before getting their pensions. Some were laid off and were told they would be taken back. Now they are being told they will not be taken on. The equipment on the C.N.R., at
