The Address-Mr. Van Horne least in the maritime provinces, is dilapidated and obsolete. Many of the buildings are falling apart. The C.N.R. has a tremendous opportunity right now to put thousands of men to work to get this equipment in better shape. I do not accuse Mr. Gordon and the Liberal-appointed Liberal directors of the C.N.R., some of whom were re-appointed by this government, includng one who was a former Liberal cabinet minister, of acting in such a way as to cause the greatest hardship for the employees of the C.N.R. and the greatest harm to this government, but I do say that they are giving that impression.
With regard to pensions for retired workers of the now government-owned railways, let us not forget that we spent 22 years in opposition berating the former government because they would not provide adequate pensions for many former C.N.R. workers. Some of those pensions are less than $30 a month. Well, here we are in office, and these men cannot wait another 22 years for this government to provide those increases while they are still living.
Old age pensions are still inadequate. When,
I ask, is this government going to take effective means to correct the injustices inflicted on so many of our older people because of the means test? You have to be poor or arrange to become poor between 65 and 70 to get the pension and you must be very careful to remain poor to keep it. Yet this government knows that it is impossible to get along on $55 a month. Why oblige and encourage, because of present legislation, our people to so arrange their afEairs that they have to have next to nothing at age 65 in order to qualify for the pension?
When are we going to get around to putting justice into invalids' pensions? Of course I realize that some provinces are more stringent than others in determining who is enough of an invalid to qualify although the regulations are uniform throughout Canada, but we still have thousands of people who cannot earn a living in their normal occupations because of invalidity and who, because of unnecessary Liberal hold-over regulations, cannot get the invalids' pension, however meagre and inadequate it is in amount.
What is needed here is a new meeting with the provinces and the definition of "invalid" broadened so that the pension will be paid to all those who, because of illness or infirmity, are unable to earn a living in their normal or usual occupation. 1 respectfully request that this be done now.
This condition of too stringent and unfair regulations, inadequate amounts and the means test applies equally to blind pensions,

widows* allowances, veterans allowances and many other groups of our unfortunate people who need help. In the case of blind persons, and I have a few so afflicted people in my riding, they probably can make $15 or $20 a week working in some pulp mill canteen but if they do so the pension is not paid to them and they do not earn enough to make a living.
I come now to family allowances. It has always been and still is my belief that family allowances represent one of the best and most equitable means of effecting a more just distribution of the wealth of the country to those who need it most and who have the greatest claim to it, our children. In determining the amount set in 1945 a yardstick had to be used. There must have been a yardstick and it had to be the value of a dollar in 1945 in relation to the cost of living in 1945. But the cost of living has in many respects doubled since then and if we were right in 1945 in setting the amount in relation to the purchasing power of a dollar then we must now. restore that purchasing power to our children and that would mean doubling family allowances. In other words, the same purchasing power must be placed in the hands of the mothers of our Canadian families. To do this means doubling the amounts and raising them to at least $12 per child. These payments should also be paid right through until the child reaches 18 years of age and then continue until that person completes his or her education.
I feel that too many members simply do not realize the hardships our children have to endure in privation and want in so many sections of the country and particularly in my own riding. It is my opinion, and it is shared by many, that as long as any government fails to restore and maintain the purchasing power of family allowances we are falling short of doing our duty towards the children of this country. I submit that this long overdue action should be taken now.
I wish to reaffirm and stress the formal demands of the government of my province made at the last sitting of the New Brunswick legislature for a royal commission to study, investigate and determine how best the Bank of Canada can serve Canada. We know it is not now fulfilling the purposes for which it was created. We know that ever since it was created high finance has been the invisible but nevertheless effective boss of the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada should be under parliament and through it under the will of all the Canadian people.
The lofty ideals which animated the leaders of government at the time the Bank of Canada was founded have, by and large, gone by the board. A return to those ideals is of

primary concern to all Canadians. The management, the regulatory powers, the workings, the actions, the results of their regulations must come under review and it is with great satisfaction that I second the request of my province for a royal commission to investigate the Bank of Canada and monetary policies generally and also request that the evidently needed changes be carried out at the earliest possible moment.
May I speak now of farming and congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for the price support program he introduced. It must be noted, however, that the minimum prices, set at 80 per cent of the average price of any one farm product over the past 10 years, produce very low prices for many farm commodities, especially potatoes, pulpwood, pork and so on. In my opinion this average is too low. It must be increased and increased now.
Last year the minister indicated, and I congratulate him for it, sweeping changes in the farm loan board and I am pleased that legislation will be introduced at this session to bring about these badly needed changes. We need many things so far as the farm loan board is concerned but we need most a farm loan board that will be a farm loan board. We need sweeping changes in the procedure and regulations so that our farmers may obtain loans for all reasonable purposes without delay and without being bogged down in red tape as they are now. It takes six months to get a loan at the present time. There is one office of the farm loan board for the whole province of New Brunswick and that office is located in Saint John. Many of my people in the county of Madawaska do not speak English and they cannot get their loans processed by people who speak their maternal tongue simply because the employees in Saint John do not speak French.
I feel that the farm loan board should be made available to all farmers for whatever reasonable purpose they need money such as the purchase of trucks and equipment, the fixing up of their farms, the buying of seed, even the buying of cars, whatever they need! Farming today is nothing more or less than a small business and the farmer is a producer just as much as the person who makes or manufactures anything is a producer. To produce, money is needed. Our farmers need money and when they need it they must have it. It is no good to them six months later because then the crisis has passed.
Our potato farmers must be placed in a position which will permit them to compete with United States dumped potatoes. A new look is needed. While a diversion price program is needed at this time, these on again,
The Address-Mr. Van Horne off again price diversion programs do not provide the security our potato farmers require and deserve.
I should like to say a word about housing. I am grateful for what the government has done to fight the recession and to help build more houses by making hundreds of millions of dollars available for housing and by reducing the down payments. But I respectfully submit that these measures, however helpful they may be in some areas, are not sufficient and do not, in my riding and in many others, solve the housing problem. Millions of our people could not afford to pay the unreasonably high down payments demanded by the former government and for the most part they cannot afford to disburse the very high down payments now demanded under present legislation. This unnecessary requirement, coupled with all the other expenses for equipment and furniture so necessary on moving into a new house, is placing housing under the National Housing Act beyond the reach of millions of Canadian families who need adequate housing in the worse way.
For three years I have been a member of the house and for three years I have pleaded again and again for the complete adoption, lock, stock and barrel, of the same type of housing legislation as exists in the United States. I ask very humbly that the Canadian government have as much confidence in the Canadian people in regard to housing as the United States government has in over 160 million Americans.
Recent amendments to the United States housing act give further aid to young families. If you talk to any real estate developer, he will tell you that by the time a young family manages to gather up the downpayment for a Canadian N.H.A. house, purchase the kitchen equipment and furniture needed, that family is usually head over heels in debt. They have so many monthly payments to make and have to pinch pennies to such an extent that their lives are made miserable for many years afterwards.
While resting up after the last election at Fort Lauderdale, Florida, I visited several United States housing projects. I brought with me some folders to give hon. members an idea of the type of houses in these projects. Here is one type of house shown near the bottom of this page. This has three very fine bedrooms, two bathrooms ahd when you walk into the kitchen you find a kitchen that is completely equipped with electric stove, refrigerator, automatic washer and dryer. This equipment is included in the total cost of the house, and the house sells for $13,100. If one is a veteran there is no

The Address-Mr. Van Horne down payment, and for the ordinary citizen the down payment is $400 and that includes the legal fees.
Do you know that in the province of Quebec, and I know whereof I speak, the down payment on a house costing $11,000 would be about $1,200 and the cost of closing, that is arranging the legal papers, is never less than $220, that is about 25 per cent of the down payment. In Canada these homes would sell for much more than $13,000. The determining factor, however, is the fact that in the United States the veteran pays nothing down and the non-veteran pays $400. The interest rate is five per cent. As I said before, this amount of $400 includes the closing fees.
The reason there is such an accelerated house-building program in the United States is that for many years a United States citizen could purchase his home with this low down payment, and he has done so. In addition, in the United States housing act loans are available in many instances for houses already built. In Canada, we have nothing like this. In many cases home owners lose their equity in their homes because, when they go to sell these homes the trust companies and insurance companies will only grant a loan up to about 50 per cent of the value. This places the purchaser in a position where he cannot find the down payment, and it is only after the owner accepts a second mortgage or some other arrangement that the owner can sell his home. My request is simple and direct.
I ask this government to place as much confidence in 18 million Canadians as the United States government places in 160 million Americans. I ask that the interest rate be reduced.
I should like to say a word now about the C.B.C. If this government ever inherited a mess, it was when we took over the C.B.C. The whole top echelon of the C.B.C. seems to be blinded by the wrong kind of liberalism. The C.B.C. is a source of more complaints than any other branch of this government. I suggest that the government sell the C.B.C. and make it completely independent of the government. It is a well established and well known fact that if one medium of information is subject to government control, however slight or indirect, all mediums like the press are automatically placed in a position where they are not entirely free from government control. So far as the men at the C.B.C. are concerned, they seem to want to go out of their way to make the C.B.C. unpopular and a source of irritation for many Canadians.
IMr. Van Home.]
I should like now to say a word about the Norman case. I very much regret that these incidents have developed-

Then I should like to say a word about oil. In the Atlantic provinces, at least, there is a well directed and well organized arrangement between the major oil companies to try to squeeze out the smaller oil companies. Here is how it works. They charge regular prices to the small gasoline and fuel oil consumer and secretly cut prices to the big oil and gasoline users. This is in restraint of trade. In the United States, all oil companies must publish their prices to both the big consumer and the small consumer. The results of these secret dealings in prices are prejudicial to the smaller companies and the smaller consumers. What Canada needs is legislation similar to that which exists in the United States whereby the oil and gasoline companies must publish their prices to the big consumers as well as to the small consumers.
This matter is of more importance than we may think because the small home owner is being forced to subsidize the piratical raids of the major oil companies who sell to the major oil and gas users at secret discounts in order to put the independent oil and gas distributing companies out of business, thereby eliminating competition. These big oil and gas companies have one price to the ordinary citizen and a secret, low price to the big user. The poor are paying through the nose so that the bigger, richer user may be subsidized and the big oil companies may squeeze out the smaller ones.
Once every ten years, sir, Canada has an opportunity to put her right foot forward and show the world what she does, how her people live, and what she has to sell, by her exhibits at these world fairs. I happened to have occasion to visit the Canadian exhibit at Brussels the other day. Signs pointing the way to the Canadian restaurant are to be seen all around the building. When you get to the Canadian restaurant, which boasts of fine Canadian foods, you cannot even get a plate of pea soup. The fellow who runs it is not a Canadian; the chef is not a Canadian; and there is not a Canadian waiter in the place. There is not a Canadian dish on the menu, and that is the Canadian restaurant.
I went down to the exhibits, and at a time when 8,000 people in my riding are out of work because we cannot sell our paper and

lumber-and this is not the fault of the government-there was not a model sawmill on exhibit. I asked one of the managers why they did not have a model sawmill on exhibition so the people would see how we make lumber.
Even a little exhibition like the one in Tatamagouche last year which I attended had a model sawmill. At Brussels fishing is represented by a few rubber and wooden fish in a great big tank. The maple syrup industry is not represented at all. There is quite a bit of mention of Eskimos. The mounted police have no horses and that fact disappoints visitors. The Indians of course are not represented at all. The pulp and paper industry is represented by three or four sheets of paper on the wall, if anybody wants to read them; but very few do so. I think that here we have an opportunity. I do not mind telling you, sir, that, comparing our exhibit with the other exhibits at that fair, you would almost think that Canada is in dire need of a Colombo plan.
But it is not too late to correct that situation. There are still five months to go. The French exhibit opened only on the Saturday that I was there which was the Saturday before last. We could correct our pavilion. We could do a great deal to tell the story of Canada to the world. Sixty million people will visit the fair. If we keep on in the way we are going there will be queues and lineups at the French pavilion, the Russian pavilion and the British pavilion but there will be no line-ups at the Canadian pavilion. We have here an opportunity to show the world what we think, what our culture is, how we live and what we must do to survive and prosper. Let us take advantage of this opportunity by making this exhibit at least a storytelling one, one that will tell the people of the world just how we live and just how we make a living.

I should like to close on a very important note. Last fall when we were over at the NATO conference in Paris we had the opportunity to witness what went on there and to learn of the advances made in many countries other than our own in the realm of education, in technilogical advances, in military science and calling for higher skills and higher training. I said there that as long as money prevented people from developing their talents and acquiring an education governments were remiss in their
The Address-Mr. Gout duties, and I believe that. Certainly it is nonsense that in this day and age, in a country so rich as Canada, hundreds of thousands of Canadian people are unable to develop the talents that God gave them, are unable to get an education, merely because they do not have the money. I think it is high time that governments in Canada get together-I refer to provincial governments and the federal government-and worked out a plan whereby any young man or woman who has the ability to learn and the desire to do so should not be denied an education because of lack of funds. Mr. Speaker, I want to associate myself with the previous speakers in tendering to you my warmest congratulations on your appointment as Speaker of the Commons for a second term.
Those among us who were here during the last parliament had the advantage to note your fairness and sound judgment, and I would like to assure you, right at the start of this session, that you will continue to receive from the members of the official opposition, every possible co-operation and respect when you endeavour to protect the rights and privileges of every hon. member, without regard to political affiliation.
I also congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Mr. Speaker, the $350 million the Liberal government had left in the treasury for the year 1956-1957, in addition to 250 million from the unemployment insurance fund, which have been spent since June 10, 1957, make up a total of 600 million we had accumulated during 22 years of Liberal administration. Business was prospering in this country and everybody agreed that it did, even the Conservatives, as my Conservative rival said during the last election in a speech he made at Navan on February 26 last, in the presence of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) who had accompanied him that night, according to the following item published by the Ottawa Citizen and the Ottawa Journal:
(Text):
Mr. Nixon and Agriculture Minister Douglas Harkness addressed some 100 supporters at Navan's arena and fought a two-hour battle to make themselves heard over the din of a hockey game in the adjoining rink.
Members of the audience at the rear of the hall actually a section of the arena, had difficulty hearing over the noise of cheering spectators, sticks banging on boards, the referee's whistle and the piercing siren to end periods.
Mr. Nixon raised his voice to declare- "We have just gone through the best 10 years Canada has ever seen".

The Address-Mr. Gour (Translation):
After only eleven months of a Conservative government there is unemployment as we have never seen before in Canada, except under a Conservative government from 1930 to 1935. The tokens of those times have been included in unemployment insurance for the past month.
Our foreign trade is in a slump and our external relations with our best customer are in a bad way.
What happened to the surplus promised by the Conservative party during the election of 1957-58? From the scant information we were able to obtain from the government about our financial situation, it seems that the promised surplus, which has been one of the reasons for the success of the Conservative party in the last election campaign, will give way to a deficit. I would not be surprised if the deficit were over $500 million for the fiscal year 1958-59. It is not so bad for a Conservative administration which was lucky enough to take office at a time when the country was prosperous and had a surplus of $350 million, as I said a moment ago, and with an unemployment insurance fund of close to $900 million, to have spent over $250 million up to now, which brings the total to $600 million. That same Conservative administration intends to submit a budget with a deficit of over $500 million. All that in the span of a year and a half.
The way things are going, if the country has the misfortune of being led by the Conservative party for four years, the deficit will then be from 4 to 5 billion.
And history is repeating itself, for every time a Conservative administration is in power, we experience a deficit and a loss of markets, and as soon as the Liberals take over, they have to pay off those debts and bring the country back to prosperity.
I have the honour of representing the fine constituency of Russell since 1945 and I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to thank all who gave me their support and who voted for me in great numbers. Since the country is in such a bad situation, I would suggest, in order to remedy unemployment in the fine constituency of Russell, two projects which were to be undertaken in 1957 had the Liberal party been returned to power. I refer to a post office in Eastview, a prosperous little town whose intelligent, hard-working and clever population numbers more than 22,000, having increased by 14,000 in the last ten years. This town is surrounded by the city of Ottawa, which means that a post office
IMr. Gour.]
would serve the Rockcliffe airport, Rideau ward-one of the finest districts of Ottawa- which includes Manor Park, Cardinal Heights, Rothwell Heights, St. Laurent Boulevard and Overbrook, comprising a population of about 40,000 people.
The second project I would suggest would be the construction of a "Pentagon" on grounds belonging to the government, part of which is in the town of Eastview, part in the city of Ottawa. This project was to be undertaken in 1957-58 by the Liberal government. This would give work to thousands of jobless in the constituency of Russell and in the constituencies of Carleton, Ottawa East, Ottawa West and Hull. It would require materials manufactured in other parts of the country.
I believe that, if the basic income tax exemption was raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for single taxpayers and from $2,000 to $3,000 for married people, low income people would then have some money left.
This would allow people to buy what they need and would incite industry to produce more and to employ more people. I believe that the government should rather encourage industrialists of any country-if they are of the Commonwealth, so much the better-to come to Canada so as to produce here most of those industrial goods which we buy abroad at this time. In this way we would give work to our people. That is what the Liberal government did and that is what brought about the prosperity which we enjoyed under a Liberal administration.
I do not think there is anything practical in the idea of diverting our purchases from one country to the other. We should rather seek to extend trade with anybody who wants to trade with us since, after all, it is the individual who buys what he likes. This is no communist country. It is not up to us to dictate to every individual the type of handkerchief, shoes, dresses, suit, home appliance, furniture, agricultural machinery or car which he or she wishes to buy. It is up to those who want to trade with us to send their representatives to inquire into our needs and then to produce those goods and arrange the prices with due regard to the conditions of our markets. We have to do the same when we trade with other countries. The following elements are generally present in any sales operations; price, quality, servicing and publicity.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) who has increased the support price on

various agricultural products. However, this is of no particular advantage to the farmer since these products usually sold at a higher price than the guaranteed price.
The support price for butter, eggs, pork and cheese should have been set at 10 per cent above what it is. Unfortunately he reduced the price of powdered milk by 2 cents a pound whereas that was the only product sold under guaranteed price by the Liberal government. This will certainly bring about loss of revenue to the farmer.
So as to allow our producers doing mixed farming to meet competition in spite of the high prices they have to pay for the products they buy, the subsidy for the transport of western grain should be raised by at least $3 a ton. Such a step would stimulate the purchase of wheat, oats, barley, rye and grain from the western provinces.
Since there is a good market for our livestock in the United States, our Eastern farmers would be encouraged to fatten their cattle rather than sell them young when they are not really ready for the market for only about half the price that the fattened livestock would bring. This would also encourage them to raise more cattle and would require more fenced-in pasture land, thus restricting the seeded acreage. Thus they would have to buy more western grain.
They should also benefit from more generous agricultural loans. At this time, it is very difficult for a farmer to establish his son on a farm. He cannot borrow the money required to buy a farm. The maximum loan on a good hundred acre farm is from 4 to 6 thousand dollars. Farmers who, for one reason or another, sell their land are looking for cash in order to buy a house in a village or a town.
I think that the percentage of the farm loan should be raised to 85 per cent of the value assessed by the commission's inspectors. Thus the number of farmers or sons of farmers who leave the farm to displace our city workers would be greatly reduced.
In concluding, I wish to ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming-) to grant, this year, at least, about thirty thousand scholarships as I find that unfortunately the great majority of our high school and university students cannot find any work this year during the summer holidays. This situation will certainly affect a great number of them who, for lack of money, will not be able to carry on their studies.
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
In the light of the new developments happening in the world, we realize, more than ever, the necessity of providing more for our young boys and girls, in order that they may have the benefit of further studies in our universities for the benefit of the future generation.
One of the best investments that the government could make would be to make available a few thousand dollars to our young students who have the talent and the will to pursue their studies but whose parents lack the necessary financial means.
I would ask the ministers concerned to kindly ponder seriously these remarks, which are made in good faith and are, to my mind, very practical in order to alleviate the present situation. This would be to the advantage not only of all Canadians, but of the present government as well.

Mr. Speaker, I join with others in congratulating you on your election to the high office you hold and I would appreciate if you would extend my congratulations to your deputy. I would also like to join with others in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I would like to incorporate and endorse all the fine remarks which have been passed in reference to you and your high office and that of your deputy, as well as those in reference to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
When I was elected as a member of parliament on March 31 last I accepted this high honour with a deep sense of humility. I accept the privilege of speaking in this debate with an even greater sense of humility being mindful of the hon. members on both sides of this house who have had much experience in parliamentary debate and also being mindful of those who have sat in this house in the past but who are not with us today.
The constituency of Bow River at one time was a part of Calgary South and I would like to call to memory, particularly for those senior members of parliament who are with us today, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett who at one time represented that part of Bow River before it got gerrymandered. I refer, of course, to Banff, Lake Louise and that territory west of Calgary. I would also like

The Address-Mr. Woolliams to bring to the attention of the senior members the late Arthur L. Smith of Calgary South who I believe by his wit and wisdom was successful on one occasion in receiving a ruling from the Speaker under which the house adjourned to permit hon. members to attend a famous football game in Toronto some years ago. I am happy to see that his son, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) is now carrying on the fine tradition of his father.
I think I would be most remiss in my duty as the member for Bow River constituency if I did not mention Mr. Charlie Johnston who represented this constituency for 23 years. For 23 years he served the constituency in the capacity of a public servant. I pay tribute to him in this house and call him to mind particularly to the minds of the senior members of this house. In passing, however, I might mention that although he represented the constituency for a long period of time, March 31 last marked the end of the Social Credit party as a force in this federal parliament. Like other small groups the members of that party never shared in national aims and objectives because they were particularly local in their viewpoint in every respect. As a coal miner from the city of Drumheller expressed it, "Alberta, as far as its rural constituencies are concerned, had built a wall around itself with respect to influence in federal affairs because it was represented by a local party from the province of Alberta.''
In listening to Social Credit speakers in the past I always found it interesting to note one of the famous questions they asked,

namely "What have the old line parties done for Canada?" I have heard the same question asked by members of the other small group, the C.C.F., when I was living in the province of Saskatchewan. My answer to that question is very simple. If one looks through the pages of Canadian history since confederation one finds that the Conservatives and Liberals have governed this country for almost equal periods of time. When the Conservatives were in power the Liberals were the official opposition and vice versa. All the development of this country, industrial, economic, political and social, has taken place either under a Conservative government when the Liberals were in opposition or under a Liberal government when the Conservatives were in opposition. I am also aware that the destruction of the Social Credit party as a force in the federal parliament will result in a saving of time in the deliberations of this house.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with another subject but I see that time is running out. May I call it ten o'clock?
On motion of Mr. Woolliams the debate was adjourned.
